 Programme, (ix) Electronics Material Development Programme and (x) Technology Missions have been clubbed with the Budget
 for TDC for better focus and optimum utilisation of funds. It may be noted that IDC budget which in 1995-96 was only Rs. 1.75
 crores had been increased to Rs. 24.17 crores in 1996-97 by clubbing the funds requirements of the above Programmes.
1.2 The Electronics industry development project is a project for man power development supported by World Bank and
 Swiss Development Cooperation. The project started in June 1991 and is coming to' an end in March 1997. Most of the
 expenditure for various activities has been incurred till 1995-96. The residual work to be completed in 1996-97 has lower
 financial requirements than in 1995-96.
1.3 The Budget provision for the Japanese language training has been curtailed keeping in view that the industry who are the
 ultimate beneficiary of this programme, should also financially contribute towards this programme.
1.4 Thus, the reduction in budgetory support in 1996-97 is not because of lack of programmes but because of lack of funds
 allocated by Planning Commission.
COMMENTS:
The Committee notes the position.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
2. While the overall staff strength is set to register a decline in 1997 as compared to 1996, it is significant to note that the
 posts in higher scales of Rs. 450~5700 and above are on the increase. The decline in the number of posts is mainly confined to
 the Pay Scale of Rs. 3700-5000 and below. This reflects the state of depression which has its bearing on the generation of
 employment.
Action taken by the Department
The Department of Electronics was set up in 1970. At the time of its inception, more posts in the lower level were filled than
 the higher one's. The Department is following the Flexible Complementing Scheme (FCS) in respect of its S&T personnel.
 Under the FCS Scheme, the promotion of S&T personnel is person oriented i.e. at the time of promotion, the lower post is

 automatically abolished and the higher post is created.' Hence, gradually the posts in the higher scales have been increasing and
 the lower grades are declining. Moreover, the Government has imposed 10% cut in the staff strength. An exercise to this effect
 was also carried out in this Department and a target of 9.61 % has been achieved by I" abolishing various posts. This is also one of

RECOMMENDATIONS:
3. The Committee strongly feels that the DOE has failed to orient itself to the changing needs of the country and development. The
 Department appears to have deviated from its directed policy and therefore it needs introspection for a suitable direction in the context
 of National development.
Action taken by the Department
The Department of Electronics has not deviated from its directed policy. With Iiberalisation of economy, DOE is placing more
 emphasis on its promotional role. As financial allocations have been drastically reduced against requirements and further because of
 the directive that no new programmes are to be supported in the last year of the 8th Plan, all the development programmes could not
 be addressed fully. However, the 9th Plan proposes several new initiatives for accelerated development of electronics.
COMMENTS
As a result of developments in science, changes take place in the field of electronics at a faster pace. Department of Electronics
 should keep itself abreast with all the developments, possess the knowledge, equipment and wherewithal to assess the utility and
 potential of such changes and be in a position to recommend what is best suited in the context of national requirements. If required it
 should be in the position to develop certain models based on the latest changes without effecting substantial changes in its production
 base and recommend the same to the industry.
RECOMMENDA TIONS:
4. The Committee observes that an amount of Rs. 10.40 crores could not be utilised due to non-materialisation of DANIDA project.
 The Committee observes that the project was not planned properly taking all the contingencies into account. This also reflects on the
 inability of the Department to utilise foreign assistance.
Action taken by the Department
The terms & conditions of DANIDA project were not acceptable to DOE both technically and financially. Firstly, the DANIDA
 project was a mixed credit/loan and not a grant-in ­-aid. Secondly, DANIDA insisted procurement of equipment impart training only
 from Denmark, wherein 60% of loan amount would have flown back to Denmark. Thirdly, the entire project management activity was
 to be handled by Danish contractor and not by STQC. Hence, DOE decided to drop the project on its own, as these terms and
 conditions were found to be not suitable.
Regarding proper utilisation of foreign assistance, it is pertinent to mention that STQC has successfully implemented the Indo-
German project for 15 years from 1980 to 1995. Even currently, another Indo-German project viz. Society for Electronics Test
 Engineering. (SETE) is being successfully implemented. This shows that STQClDOE is able to utilise foreign assistance effectively,
 provided the terms and Conditions are favourable to the Indian Government.
COMMENTS:
The Committee feels that Department of Electronics should have, before accepting the project, seen through the terms and
 conditions carefully. It should have declined the offer ab initio if it did not suit us instead of first accepting and then dithering on the
 same. In future, greater care should be taken in accepting the foreign projects and national interest should be uppermost in our 'minds.
RECOMMENDA TIONS:
5 (a): There has been significant increase in the operational expanses (Plan as well as Non-Plan) of Electronics Regional Test
 Laboratories. The actual expenditure was Rs. 3.12 crores (Plan) and Rs. 1.17 crores (Non-Plan) in 1994-95. It went up to Rs. 3.26
 crores (Plan) and Rs. 1.40 crores (Non-Plan) and remained at that level in the revised estimates for 1995-96. The budget estimates
 for 1996-97 provide Rs. 3.75 crores (Plan) and Rs. 1.40 crores (Non-Plan). The Committee feels there is need to check the Non-
Plan expenditure. Same is the case in respect of operational expenses of Electronics and Test and Development centres.
(b): The Committee feels that there is need to make such laboratories and test centres self supporting. They should provide test
 facilities on commercial basis instead of depending on budgetary support.

(a): The reasons for increase in the operational expenditure (Plan as well as Non-Plan) of Electronics Regional Test Laboratories

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development on the recommendations
 contained in the Thirty-fifth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
 Environment and Forests on the Demands for Grants (1996-97) of the Department of Ocean Development which was presented to the
 Rajya Sabha on 4th September, 1996. There are 6 recommendations contained in the Thirty-fifth Report of the Committee. Action
 Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee, were received from the Department on 16th January, 1997.
On scrutiny of the Action Taken Report as received from the Department of Biotechnology, the Committee finds that two
 recommendations have been fully implemented. The Committee in regard to its recommendation Nos. 23 & 26 recommends that the
 Department should make out a strong case for enhance allocation and improve its own resource generation wherever feasible. In
 regard to recommendation No. 30 the Department should take steps to complete the survey expeditiously. The Committee in regard to
 its recommendation No. 28 observes that the Department may continue with the existing system of charting the vessel for its
 Antarctica operation.
The Committee's recommendation, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the Department
 of Ocean Development are given in the succeeding paragraphs:-
RECOMMENDATION
"The Committee feels that the Department should make out a strong case for enhancement in its allocations in the revised
 estimates for the current year".
(Para No. 23)
Action Taken 
by the Department
The B.E. for 1996-97 for the Department was approved as follows:
Plan: Rs. 52.00 crores
Non Plan: Rs. 14.83 crores
The Department 
vide its communication No. DOD/52-IFD/28/96 dated 17.10.1996 requested Ministry of Finance for the
 following enhanced allocation at RE. stage for 1996­97:-
Plan: Rs. 58.47 crores
Non Plan: Rs. 19.77 crores
A meeting was taken by Secretary (Expn.) with the Financial Adviser of the Department on 22.10.1996 wherein it was desired by
 Secretary (Expn.) that the Department should endeavour to generate a saving of Rs. 10 crores under Plan so that R.E. for 1996-97 is
 reduced to Rs. 42 crores in view of overall resource constraints being faced by the Govt. of India. An exercise was made to locate
 savings under Plan side. However, it was found that Rs. 51.55 crores will be the minimum requirement to carry out the essential
 components of the various programmes. Accordingly, the Department sent a revised proposal requesting for the allocation of Rs.
 51.55 crores on the Plan side at RE. 1996-97. However, Finance Ministry have communicated the following size of the RE. for the
 Department for 1996-97.
Plan: Rs. 45 crores
Non Plan: Rs. 19.38 crores
1
2
While higher allocation under Non-Plan was allowed in order to cle21r the arrears of Shipping Corporation of India, Bombay,
 towards running and maintenance of Research Vessels, Sagar Kanya and Sagar Sampada, outlay on Plan side was reduced
 substantially.
As a whole, the total (Plan and Non-Plan) allocation has been reduced from Rs. 66.83 crores to Rs. 64.38 crores.
Inspite of Department's best efforts allocation under Plan side could not be enhanced due to resource constraints.
COMMENTS:
The Committee feels that the Department should make out its case for enhanced allocation for the financial year 1997-98. At the
 same time it should try to improve its own resource generation wherever feasible.

"The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department should get what it had originally projected 
i.e. a sum of Rs. 23
 crores".
(Para No. 25)

 constrained to keep the allocation for Antarctic Research at Rs. 20 crores only. However, we are seeking an additional allocation of
 Rs. 2.8 crores in the second supplementary.

Exploitation of Krill, Resources
"Besides, the Department should endeavour for commercial exploitation of the krill fishery and other such resources in the
 Antarctic waters because of its demand in the overseas markets."
(Para No. 25)
Action taken by the Department
The Department took up the first expedition to Antarctic waters for exploration of the potential of krill and other Marine Living
 Resources, with a view to assess the economic viability of future commercial exploitation of these resources. Two representatives of
 Fishing Industry also participated in this cruise to have a first hand information on the potential of krill and other living resources in
 the Antarctic waters. The product development from the krill stock harvested and brought to the main land is in progress. Some of the
 frozen, dried and canned products have already been produced and test marketed. The first exclusive Antarctic cruise for assessment
 of krill and other living resources was confined only to fishing area 58 of the Antarctic waters and that too in the summer months. For
 establishing the commercial feasibility to exploit krill, there is a necessity to undertake such studies even during the winter season,
 which will require a larger and sophisticated vessel with onboard processing facilities and a fish hold capacity of over 500 to 800
 tonnes at minus 40° C. The preliminary assessment worked out so far indicates that at present it is not commercially viable.

ACQUISITION ON AN' ICEBREAKERIMULTIPURPOSE OCEANOGRAPHIC RESEARCH VESSEL
The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests
 in its 35th Report on Demands for Grants 1996-97 of the Department of Ocean Development has recommended that
 the Department should work out the economics of all the alternatives to acquire, including the purchase of a new vessel
 and plan its strategy accordingly, and further that the Committee should be apprised of economics of all the proposals.
The specifications of an Icebreaker-cum-Multipurpose vessel was drawn up by an Expert Group constituted by the
 Department and was circulated in the international market in 1994. However, no offer was received which conform'
 precisely to our specifications. In the meantime, in view of the then political scenario in Russia, an Expert Group
 visited Russia for a market survey. The Expert Group had a meeting with the Chief Expert of the Russian Federal

 designed and built and may cost anything between US $s 150 to 300 million, depending upon various fitments.
 Accordingly, the alternative of buying a second hand vessel capable of Antarctic voyage and thereafter, with
 modifications for other oceanographic research was pursued. However, Russia could not offer such a second hand
 vessel meeting our requirements.
Following the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee, yet another attempt was made to explore the
 availability of any suitable second hand vessel.
The results of our enquiry are as follows:
1.    There is a vessel under construction in Germany and will cost around 76 million DM or in other words around
 Rs. 150 crores. The requirements of any modifications for our work has not been explored.
(b) Two old vessels, namely, (1) CARIBOO and (2) LIVONIA are available. The CARIBOO would cost around
 US $s 8 million (around Rs. 30 crores); whereas LIVONIA may cost 20 million US $s (around Rs. 70 crores);
(c) The offers. of these second hand vessels received do not indicate the helipad specifications and modifications
 may include helipad construction also. Further, as per the present Antarctic requirements, the vessel should be
 capable of accommodating around 65 persons in each Expedition. These vessels do not meet our requirements.
2. Against the above background, the broad economics are as follows:-
(a) Considering the lowest offer of a second hand vessel of around Rs. 30 crores only, even without any
 modification requirements, would mean an additional annual maintenance charges of atleast Rs. 10 crores per
 annum, based on the experience of ORV Sagar Kanya.
(b) . The Antarctic Expeditions leave in December and return to India towards the end of March. If it has to be
 used for oceanographic survey, the same has to be carried out between April and October. During this period,
 the period of monsoons also overlap.
(c) Even assuming that some oceanographic work is possible, the ship will have to be mobilised after proper dry
 docking etc. and made· ready for the Antarctic Expedition. It is likely that about one month of ship time will
 be lost in the process and additional expenditure incurred. In other words, in practical terns, the vessel would
 be utilised only for Antarctic expeditions.

Present Arrangement for Antarctic Expeditions:-
The Department has entered into a three year charter covering upto 1997-1998 season. The total charter cost per annum is around
 Rs. 9 crores approximately.
The chartering of a vessel providing their own officers and crew. The Department's budget is limited and the present budget does
 not allow for purchase of new vessel costing around Rs. 150 crores or more. In fact the present budget does not also allow even
 investments of the order of Rs. 30 crores besides additional operational and maintenance costs.     
On the other hand chartering of a vessel on an average of around Rs. 10 crores per annum would meet our Antarctic requirements
 and does not cost any additional investment on employment, maintenance, operational costs, spares, dry docking, etc. Acquisition of a
 second hand vessel and modifications cannot make it all purpose and will have limited functions only. In the event the future Antarctic
 programme involves going to Rose Sea or other difficult areas of Antarctica, it would be necessary to deploy an Icebreaker rather than
 Ice Class vessels, such as CARIBOO 
or LIVONIA.
Taking the overall considerations, as desired by Secretary DOD, a joint meeting of JS, JS & FA and Adviser was convened to
 examine this issue. The meeting arrives at the following conclusions:
(a)    Purchase of an Icebreaker, as per our specifications, is not economically viable.
(b)    (b) the option of a purchase of second hand vessel and further modifications will not prove to be more cost effective than the
 present arrangement for chartering the vessel for the Antarctic Expedition;
(c) The Department already has ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar Sampada. In addition, it has recently commissioned a CRV
 Sagar Paschmi. Another CRV is expected to be commissioned very soon.

REPORT
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its
 behalf, present this Forty-sixth Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Science & Technology (Ministry of Science & Technology) for the
 year 1997-98 (Demand No. 74).
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 2nd April, 1997 the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Science & Technology gave an overview of
 the various activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the Department particularly in the fields of
 Basic Research and allied­areas and their financial aspects.
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Officers of the Department of Science & Technology for their cooperation answering the queries raised by
 Members on various aspects on programmes initiated by the Department.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 22nd April, 1997.
5. The Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, in his presentation before the Committee gave an overview of the thrust areas in which the Department
 is engaged in pursuance of the national objective of making scientific and technological progress for attaining self-reliance. Over the years, the Department and
 autonomous institutions under the Department of Science and Technology have been making consistent efforts in formulation of policy statements and guidelines on
 Science and Technology; promotion of new areas of scientific research; Co-ordination of inter-departmental Science and Technological efforts; Support basic and
 applied research in universities/labs/institutions; International Science and Technology co-operation; Support high quality research in autonomous bodies; Catalysing
 Science and Technology interaction in societal programmes, entrepreneurship development; Science popularisation, communication and Science and Technology
 Management Information System; Promotion of commercialisation of home grown technology; support to technology development programmes, technology
 information and assessment; providing scientific services in the areas of Surveying and Mapping through its autonomous organisations e.g. Survey of India (SOl) and
 National Atlas Thematic and Mapping Organisations (NATMO); Meteorology through India Meteorological Department and National Centre for Medium Range
 Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) and Technology Development Board (TDB).
6. After listening to the presentation made by the Secretary, Department of Science and Technology, the Committee examined the budgetary allocation of the
 Department for the year 1997-98* While considering the Demands for Grants of the Department, the Committee had an opportunity to review the work of various
 projects and programmes which fall within the mandate of the Department.
7. The Budget Estimates of 1997-98 have registered an increase from Rs. 242.55 crores in the previous year to Rs. 268.00 crores on plan side and from Rs. 238.50
 crores to Rs. 291.87 crores on Non-Plan side. The increase in Plan provision of 1997-98 as compared to RE 1996­97 is mainly due to undertaking of increased Plan
 activities under Technology Missions, India Meteorological Department, Integrated Long Term Programme of Cooperation in S&T between India and the Republics
 of Commonwealth of Independent States; enhanced financial support to Autonomous Institutions and Professional bodies.
_____________________________________________________________________________
• For Summary of the Demands for Grants see schedule.
8. The Secretary informed the Committee that in the field of international co-operation, there are three types of programmes viz., Integrated long-term programme
 of co-operation in Science & Technology with India and Republic of Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), programmes of co-operation with the developed
 countries and lastly technical co­operation with the developing countries. Among the foremost areas in which the Government have co-operation with CIS countries
 are material technology, bio-technology, energy related issues and information technology. The Secretary further informed that they were facing some problems
 because of severe financial crunch existing in CIS countries whereas with developed countries they have equal partnership.
9. The Committee is of the view that the Department should devise programmes in such a way so that international co-operation in the field of Science and
 Technology will enable us to establish technology information centres in the long run which may facilitate not only training of our scientific community but will also
 lead to creation of centres with basic infrastructure in the field of research.
9.1 The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier recommendations as contained in its 41st report that the scientists of CIS countries today are migrating to
 developed countries in search of better opportunities. The Department should devise some programmes whereby their services could be utilised productively. The
 Committee recommends that the Department should not only bear all the expenses of the scientists who give us technology and blue-print, but also should devise a
 compensation package for them.
9.2 The Committee observes that at the same time Science & Technology has vast scope in the development of a country. Invention of a wheel has solved many
 of the problems facing the mankind which has brought tremendous transformation in the pattern of iudustrialisation of countries. As the nation progresses they come
 across problems in simplifying industrial processes and solving technological problems that have never cropped up earlier.
9.3 Level of development of a country in the field of Science & Technology plays a vital role in solving these problems and the ones that may crop up. It is
 therefore necessary to ensure rapid development in the field of technology which can be brought about by the trained work force available in the country.
9.4 Technical development would require adequate infrastructure in the form of laboratories, technical institutions and building of a scientific temper in the
 country. Latter is correlated with the former as much as former is with the latter.
9.5 The Committee in its 38th report recognised the need for developing infrastructure in the form of laboratories and technical institutions which should be
 accessible to lay men and student community for experimenting their ideas in different fields of technology. The Committee reiterates that DST should make a sincere
 beginning by initiating steps for making available a few existing laboratories to students and lay men alike under the supervision of officers and staff managing these
 laboratories. At best these laboratories could, to begin with, charge nominal fees for their use. So far as students are concerned they should be encouraged to use these
 laboratories without making any payment.
10. The Committee was informed that the mandate of the Technology Development Board (TDB) is to commercialise indigenously developed technologies on
 large-scale application of imported technologies having a commercial angle to it. The Secretary also informed the Committee that after evaluation of some 50 odd
 proposals nearly 5 of them have already been cleared and financial help has already been released.
The Committee feels satisfied that the Technology Department Board has finally sanctioned some of the projects and recommends that the Department should
 ensure that the funds allocated to TDB should be fully utilised in the current year which may facilitate R&D linkages with industry as well as be a source of revenue
 for future technological innovation.
11. While the Committee seeks to ensure that the Department of Science and Technology is not starved of funds in order to carry out its scientific and research
 programmes, the attention of the Committee was invited to some of the audit observations regarding non-receipt of utilisation-certificates to the tune of Rs. 11,553
 crores since 1977. The Secretary informed the Committee that a special drive was launched in the present year and as of 1995-96 there were no pending utilisation
 certificates.
12. The Committee is of the view that the Department should immediately stop release of funds to grants-in-aid institutions unless pending utilisation certificates
 of the current year duly certified are made available.
13. The Committee observes that' the demand made by the department under Societal programmes is Rs. 20.00 crores as compared to Rs. 26.02 crores last year.
 The Committee is of the view that the DST should explore the possibility of implementation of these programmes through networking with their scheme jointly with
 other Ministries/Departments.
14. As regards the Demands for India Meteorological Department (IMD) the Committee is of the view that they are inadequate. The functioning of the
 Department has to be more accurate and the reports have to be updated. It has been observed that Department's failure in its predictions are attributed to change in
 climatic conditions. The Committee is strongly of the view that the Department should improve its system so that it can update the information and provide accurate
 predictions as far as possible and well in time.
15. The Department, the Committee  was informed, was conscious of the problem of industrial pollution. The Department was carrying out National leather
 mission to achieve efficiency in sewage treatment in leather industries. Another project initiated is that of use of natural gas instead of coal-based energy sources and
 the research was being conducted by National Meteorological Laboratory.
The Committee is of the view that DST should encourage R&D institutions to look at problems of industrial pollution which are specific to individual
 areas1ndustries and come out with solutions.
16. The Secretary while explaining the question of linkage between R&D and user community outlined some achievements e.g. the Bose Institute, Calcutta in
 regard to its wave particle duality in the filed of Photon scatering in physics; Agharkar Research Institute, Pune's contribution in development of disease-resistant
 wheat and soyabean and the development of heart-valve by Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences & Technology, Thiruvananthapuram, etc.

 of Ocean Development to formulate plan proposals for the 9th Five Year Plan. The working group
 kept in mind the views of six expert groups which had been set up by the Department to draw
 up a 10 year perspective plan keeping in view the vital role oceans could play. The annual plan
 1997-98 is based on these reports and recommendations.
8. The Plan outlay for the Department for 1997-98 is Rs. 88.10 crores. Besides, it has been
 provided with non-plan outlay of Rs. 17.85 crores. The department would thus have a total outlay
 of Rs. 105.95 crores against the revised estimates of Rs. 64.38 crores (Plan as well as non-
Plan) in 1996-97 whereas the actual expenditure for the year was Rs. 64.08 crores. The figure
 shows a substantial increase of Rs. 41.57 crores as compared to R.E. for 1996-97. Though the
 Plan component shows an escalation of Rs. 36.10 crores in the budgetary outlay of 1997-98, the
 non-Plan component shows an increase of a sum of Rs. 3.02 crores as compared to that of
 1996-97. The Plan sector outlay for 1995-96 and 1996-97 was Rs. 52 crores each year is Rs.
 88.10 crores for 1997-98. As in the previous year the emphasis is more on Antarctic Research
 Programme during the current year. The comparative figures in terms of allocation for various
 programmes of the Department for 1994-95, 1995-96 and 1996-97 are set out in Annexure-I. The
 details of the budgetary provision for the year 1997-98 is given at Annexure-II.  
Sampada are operated and maintained by the Shipping Corporation of India- a Government of
 India Undertaking. As of 31.3.1997, the payment arrears stand at about Rs. 5.62 crore. During
 the year 1997-98, the ship operation and maintenance are likely to cost Rs. 17.6 crore. With the
 budgetary provision of Rs. 14.5 crore for the year 1997-98, Rs. 8.72 crores may spill over to
 1998-99.
12.4 The Committee observes that a sum of Rs. 3 crores is proposed to be spent on coastal
 research vessels against Rs. 1.40 crores spent last year. The Department was asked (see Q. 9
 in the questionnaire) about the kind of information the coastal research vessels have so far
 provided and how the information has been utilised. It was stated 
inter-alia that the coastal
 research vessels namely Sagar Paschimi and Sagar Purvi have provided facilities for collection
 and analysis of sea water, plankton, rediment and biological samples for the COMAPS
 programme. In case of Mumbai, the vessel facilitated collection of samples for utilisation by the

13. The Committee observes that if the collection of samples from sea is the task assigned to the
 Coastal Research Vessels including Sagar Kanya and Sagar Sampada it is a costly exercise
 aimed at draining out the resources of National exchequer. The task can be performed by
 traditional means at a far less cost. The Committee feels that it is time that the operations of

ANTARCTIC RESEARCH PROGRAMME: 
14. Much has already been mentioned about the Antarctic Programme and its scientific expeditions
 on annual basis. The first Indian research station, Dakshin Gangotri was commissioned in 1983
 and replaced in 1988 by the indigenously designed second Indian permanent station 'Maitri' which
 has adequate infrastructural facilities for conducting scientific research of contemporary nature in
 the icy continent.
14.1 Even while using Antarctica as a platform for conducting scientific experiments, India has
 always recognised the importance of preserving the pristine nature of this remote and unique
 continent. In order to uphold this commitment, India, an original not any of the Protocol on
 Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, has ratified this protocol in April, 1996.
14.2 During the period 1997-98, the Seventeenth Indian Antarctic Expedition would be launched to
 continue contemporary research in polar science with special emphasis on International
 collaboration.
14.3 The board scientific activities planned to be taken include-Continuation of studies on ozone,
 trace gases and aerosols of the Antarctic atmosphere using various state-of-the-art equipment and
 Archieval of meteorological parameters that can be employed for climate modelling and prediction
 apart from in situ geological and air-borne geophysical investigations of the Central Dronning
 Maudland area.
14.4 The Department also propose to experiments in solar terrestrial phenomenon like optical
 aurora and geo-magnetic pertubations and Survey and assessment of living resource potentials of
 Antarctic waters.
14.5 The Committee was informed that Application and utilisation of clean energy sources like

conference-cum-computer room at Maitri, during 1997-98.

 made by the Government at the international fora, it however ,feels that the Department should
 manage with the existing outlay approved. The Committee also feels the need to review the
 programme periodically to ensure that it continues to be in the interest of the country.
 
POLYMETALLIC NODULES PROGRAMME:
 
16. In 1987, Indian became the first Pionear Investor and started the Polymetallic Nodules
 Programme. The International Seabed Authority allocated 150,000 sq. km. in the Central Indian
 Ocean Basin.
16.1. The Committee was informed that at the current state of technology, land based resources
 availability and market demand, it is not economical to go in for exploitation of minerals from
 deep sea. The international Studies indicate a scope for such exploitation in 2010 or so. The
 Department plans to develop and demonstrate adequate technical capabilities in all technical
 areas of Polymetallic nodules exploitation, so that India would be ready to embark upon a
 commercial venture when it is economically viable and would not lag behind other pioneer
 investors in the world.
16.2. The Committee was further apprised that it was a national programme with international
 commitments. The four major activities under this programme were (i) Survey and exploitation of
 poly-metallic nodules; (ii) Development of mining of nodules; 
(Hi) extraction of metals; and (iv)

 Five Year Plan period against the approved outlay of Rs. 30 crores.
17. The Committee observes that the Polymetallic Nodules Programme has a long gestation period
 and would be economically viable in the year 2010. The Committee apprehends that with such a
 long gestation period the technology as also the results likely to be achieved are likely to be
 rendered obsolete and outdated. The Committee therefore recommends that to begin with a

DRUGS FROM THE SEA
 
18. The Committee was informed that though· it was an ongoing programme on development of
 drugs which was till now being funded tinder Research and Development Programme. The
 programme was scheduled for three stages. Stage-I was implemented with a total outlay of Rs.
 1.72 crores; Phase II was initiated in 1993-94 involving a total expenditure of Rs.4. 78 crores and
 would be implemented over a period of three years. The Committee was further informed that by
 the end of second phase of the project in 1995-96, over 450 different species of potential flora
 and fauna had been collected and identified and about 1200 samples were subjected to biological
 screening for ability in treating different investigations have led to identification of human
 diseases. These are 17 most promising organisms possessing anti-diabetic, anti-viral, anti-
amoebic, anti-anxiety, anti-amalarial, anti­fertility, anti-hypertensive, anti-inflammatory,
 hepatoprotective activities.
 
18.1. During 1996-97, Phase-III of the project has been initiated as the next sequential step for
 drug development. During this phase, 5 out of the 17 most potential marine organisms
 possesssing anti-viral, anti-amoebic, anti-diabetic, anti-anxiety and larvicidal properties, were taken
 up on priority basis for extracting 1-2 herbal drugs by the end of Phase- III. It is expected that
 by 1998-99, one or two herbal drugs would be available for marketing, after completion of
 regulatory pharmacological and toxicological studies.

COMPAS PROGRAMMES
 
20. The Department is operating a programme namely Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction
 Systems (COMPAS) since 1991. The COMPAS programme at present deals with the chemical,
 biological and microbiological parameters and would continue at the present level as far as the
 chemical and biological parameters are concerned. During 1991-98, microbiology programmes
 would be expanded in corporating therein physical oceanographic studies in order to make the
 programme more comprehensive. Besides, pollutants would be monitored in ecologically sensitive
 areas like Gulf of Kutch wherein large-scale developmental activities are being planned. The
 Planning Commission has approved an outlay of Rs. 4 crores for 1997-98 whereas anticipated
 expenditure would be Rs. 8.5 crores. Under this programme, levels of pollution would be
 monitored at 77 locations along the coastal areas of the country. Data in respect of 25
 parameters including nutrients, heavy metals, pesticides, pathogenic bacteria were being collected
 in 0.25 km. transact in the sea at these locations with the help of 11 Research Institutions. The
 programme was being monitored by a Steering Committee headed by the Chairman of Central
 Pollution Control Board and all the Coastal State Pollution Control Boards (PCBs) are represented
 in the Committee. Periodical exchange of data collected upto the year 1996 reveals that the sea
 approx, beyond 2 km. except off Mumbai is clean. In case of Mumbai the sea approx. beyond 5
 km. is clean.
20,1 It has further been revealed that the pollution levels in Versova, Mahim, Kakinada canal and
 Vishakapatnam harbour in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Orissa are areas of concern. The pollution
 in these areas have reached significant levels.
20.2 The data and information relating to the rising trends of pollution at the observed locations

 empowered under the Water Act (1974) and Environment Protection Act (1976) to take preventive

20.3 In the Bombay high, ONGC is carrying out exploration and exploitation of oil and natural gas.

21. The Committee is alarmed over the magnitude of marine pollution and the inadequate steps
 taken to prevent as well as control the same. The Committee finds it difficult to believe the data

 Mumbai suggests that which travelling towards Mumbai High for about 30 to 40 minutes the layer

 having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present the Forty-
Eighth Report on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Ministry of Environment and Forests for
 the year 1997-98 (Demand No. 22).

 Ministry on the basis of documents made available and the submissions made before it by the
 Secretary and other officers of the Ministry.

5. The Ministry of Environment and Forests is responsible for planning, promotion and co­ordination
 of environmental and forestry programmes. The main activities of the Ministry are conservation and
 control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas and protection of environment.
 These tasks are sought to be fulfilled through environmental impact assessment; eco-regeneration;
 assistance to organisations implementing environmental and forestry programmes; enactment of
 environmental legislation; formulation of environmental policies; promotion of environmental and
 forestry research, extension, education and training to augment the requisite manpower;
 dissemination of environmental awareness among all sectors of the country's population .
.
6. India has a land frontier of 15,200 kms. and its sea coast runs to 6100 kms. It is the second
most populous and seventh largest country in the world. The total geographical area of the country is
 3.28 million Sq. Kms. The total forest area in the country is 0.76 million Sq. Kms. which constitutes
 23.2% of the total geographical area. The percentage of actual forest of geographical area is 19.5.
 According to the National Forest Policy, 1988 33% of the total geographical area of the country
 should be under forest cover.
6.1 The Committee has been informed that Government propose to achieve the national goal-
minimum of 33% of the total land area of the country under forest cover. If, for some unavoidable
 reasons, any State cannot achieve this norm, the forest cover should not be less than 20 per cent
 of the total land area in the State and those districts which have less than 1 per cent of the
 geographical area under the forest should achieve 2% during the Ninth Plan period. In the hilly
 regions; the aim would be to maintain atleast 60% of the land area under tree cover.
6.2 The Committee has also been informed that special efforts would be made to contain the
 continued trend of diversion of forest land for non-forest activities. All existing forest-based industries
 would be encouraged to raise on their own the raw material needed by them. Private sector
 participation is sought to be encouraged for afforesting degraded and denuded lands.
7. The Ministry has also been made responsible for environment and ecology, including environment
 in coastal waters, mangroves and coral reefs, excluding marine environment on the high seas: The
 prevention of cruelty to Animals, Public Liability Insurance, Biosphere Reserves Programmes,.
 National Forest Policy and Forestry development in the country, including Social Forestry: Forest

 and many other are rapidly deteriorating. The cause of this rapid deterioration is the result of a
 number of factors a few of them being the bad vehicular technology, poor fuel quality, non-existent
 traffic planning etc.
21.1 In case of Delhi alone levels of carbon monoxide at all the traffic intersections are higher than
 the prescribed standards. It appears that the city is getting poisoned with every passing day due to

 of coal for domestic purposes. Over 200 metric tonne of Pollutant are emitted in the atmosphere

carbons and sulphur dioxide. While in November, 1995 the CO level was about 8000 micrograms, in

38. During the 1980s, the seriousness of the increasing impacts of human intervention in wildlife
 habitats became significantly noticeable in terms of fragmentation and degradation of the forests in

 domestic stock 
vis-a-vis wild animals also became manifested in terms of gradual increase in direct
 confrontations, particularly so in the case of the wild elephants and the human population in and
 around their habitats. The seriousness of the concern .was voiced by eminent wildlife

 resulted in the constitution of a Task Force by the Government of India for looking into the problems

 habitats in the country;
(ii) Conservation, protection and where necessary, restoration of the elephant range and traditional
 corridors used by the elephant population;
(iii) Development of a viable mechanism to ensure inter-state, regional and national level coordination
 in protecting and conserving the elephant and its range; and
(iv) Reduction of man-elephant conflict and development of compassion and tolerance of people
 towards elephants.

REPORT
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests having been authorised by
 the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present this Forty-eighth Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining
 to the Department of Electronics for the year 1997-98 (Demand No. 90).
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 15th April, 1997, the Secretary and other officers of the Department
 of Electronics gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Committee Sought clarifications on
 various aspects  of the performance of the Department particularly in the field of electronics programme and related
 aspects to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of the Department of Electronics for their cooperation
 and answering the queries raised by Members on various aspects on programmes initiated by the Department.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 28th April, 1997.
5. Electronics is the backbone of the entire industrial activity. It is the fastest growing sector of the industry.
 Department of Electronics (DoE) is entrusted with the task of formulation, implementation and review of policies in the
 field of electronics. It is the promotional department of the Government of India committed to development of Indian
 industry and applications of Information Technology and Electronics in the general walk of life in the country. DoE
 undertakes technology forecasting exercise which have an impact on society. Computer networking was one such area
 identified 10 yean ago by the Department before it was perceived by. other agencies in the Country. In a similar
 approach the Department initiated a programme called ERNET (Educational Research Network) to focus on
 development of national capability in computer network in the country. It has led to the movement similar to Internet
 which was infact not known in those days. DoE has played a pioneering role in introducing E-Mail and subsequently
 providing it for the country.
6. DoT (Department of Telecommunications) and DoE au complimentary agencies in furthering the total area on
 Information Technology (IT), electronics and telecommunications. While DoE is the promotional agency' for

COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/49threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:05]
 electronics in the country, Department of Telecommunications is the nodal agency in the field of telecommunications
 and it has played a big role ia tile development of telecommunications in the country. Therefore, the two agencies have
 to· work together to cover the technology level in telecommunications and IT electronics.
7. DoE has one attached office of Standardisation Testing. and Quality Certification Directorate, three public sector
 undertakings namely Computer Maintenance Corporation (CMC), Electronics Trade and Technology, Development
 Corporation Ltd. (ET&T), and Semi Conductor Complex Limited (SCL). Besides, a  large number  of Autonomous
 Bodies/Registered Societies including  C-DAC, ER&DC, STPI,  SAMEER, CEDT, DOEACC, NCST.  DoE also has a
 large outfit of STQC laboratories allover the country. These agencies act as the arms of the Department in fulfilling its
 goals.
8. The Department of Electronics is entrusted with the task of formulation and review of national policies in the field
 of electronics. The objectives of the Department are (i) to provide a focal point for Government's attention to electronic
 sector and also to act as a coordinator within and outside the Government, (ii) to bring the benefit of electronics to every
 walk of life in the country and (Hi) to make the Indian electronics industry a global player. The major programmes of
 the Department are in the field of (i) Technology Development and (ii) Industrial electronics Promotional Programme .
. 9. The Department has a budget provision contained in its Demand No. 89 for 1997-98 as follows:-

10. The Committee was informed that Electronics and Information Technology was fast becoming the largest sector
 for increasing productivity in the factories, offices and home. One rupee invested; in this sector has the capacity to
 double every two years through the benefit of higher productivity in all other sectors through automation equipment,
 instrumentation and computer control systems. Major investment to the tune of Rs. 5,000 crores during VIII Plan took
 place in areas of consumer electronics, computer, communication and broadcasting, strategic electronics, components
 and materials. During the IX Plan, the investment requirement is estimated at Rs. 29,000 crores. It would be largely met
 by private and corporate sector with Government investment playing a facilitator's role.
11. Regarding the employment generation by ,the electronics industry, the Committee was informed that presently
 the capacity was about eight lakhs and was expected to be about 21 lakhs by the year 2001-02, with a productivity
 growth of about 10%. Department of Electronics has been implementing a number of programmes to strengthen
 manpower development for electronics industry. Project IMPACT, which covers 32 participating institutes and 5
 Resource Centres, is spearheading high quality and industry-oriented education in electronics and computers in the
 country. The programme on Development of Manpower for computers has enabled initiation of computer courses in
 over 250 institutions all over the country. In order to involve the private sector in the manpower development efforts for
 computers and to ensure high quality training by private institutions, a scheme known as DOEACC is being
 implemented. Under the scheme which is approved by All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), institutes
 meeting the norms and standards laid down are given accreditation. for conducting computer courses of various levels
 viz., '0' level (foundation course), 'A' level (Diploma), 'D' level (Graduate) and 'c' level (postgraduate). In order to create
 awareness and develop elementary knowledge in computer among school students, a programme called CLASS
 (Computer literacy and Studies in School) is being implemented jointly with Ministry of Human Resource Development.
 About 3,000 schools are implementing the programme.
12. Training of teacher has been an important component of DoE initiative for manpower development. Further, a
 large number of industry professionals have been trained through continuing education schemes, workshops and
 seminars. Seven Centres of Electronics Design and Technology have been set up for imparting training in design and

 manufacturing aspects of electronic products and to strengthen electronics industry in· their respective regions.
13. The growth of electronics industry is the fastest sector of the Indian economy. It is likely to grow at a cumulative
 growth rate of 22% during the Eighth Plan as against targeted 27.7%. In the terminal year 1996-97, the total production
 would be Rs. 48,410 crores as against Eighth Plan target of Rs. 36,000 crores. The cumulative rate of growth of
 Electronics hardware in going to be about 17.4% with terminal year estimates of Rs. 22,110 crores as against WI Plan
 target of Rs, 33,400 Crores having cumulative growth rate of 27%. The Consumer Electro11ics is growing, @15.1%;
 Industrial Electronics @ 14.1%; Computer Systems @2S.8%; Communication and Broadcasting Equipment @ 19.9%.
 The production of Electronic components is likely to grow at 17.2%. The Export Oriented Electronics hardware would
 be growing @ 36.5%. The electronics production and exports alongwith Cumulative Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) in
 various sub-sector of electronics industry in the terminal year of VIII and IX Plans are appended (Appendix-II).
14. Regarding consumer electronics, the Committee was informed that it is an important segment of electronics
 industry in India as it accounts forabout 30% of the total electronic hardware production in the country, Production of
 the Consumer Electronics has increased from Rs. 3,300 crores during 1992-93 to Rs. 5,400 crores in 1995-96. In the
 terminal year of the VITI Plan, production of Rs. 6,250 crores is anticipated. Achievement of the revised target is 80% .
14.1 Production of radio received is under estimated. Based on the radio packs supplied by the industry, it is
 estimated to be 7.5-8.0 million during 1995-96. In case of 'IV, shortfall in production is due to high prices arising out of
 the devaluation of Rupee in 1991, high excise levies and also high sales tax rates. During 1995-96 CTVproduction was
 1.8 million sets whereas production of B/W 'IV was 5.6 . million sets.
14.2 Demand and hence production of radio/TV sets is closely linked with quality of software on the respective
 media. While considerable improvements have been made in the programme content/duration/choice of programmes in
 case of 1V, improvements in radio programmes are yet to take place. In this context widespread PM coverage is
 important. Items exported are BIW and colour 1V, clocks, watches and pre-recorded audio/video cassettes.
15. The industrial electronics sector continues to playa vital role for modernization through instrumentation and
 '8~tomation in India's manufacturing, public utility service and infrastructure sector. Major industrial manufacturing
 sector such as steel, cement, fertilizer, chemicals, petrochemicals, textile, jute, metal processing and fabrication,
 industrial castings, leather are some of the technology for improvement in productivity, cost efficiency, safety etc. Large
 service sectoD like railways, power are also major beneficiaries and have contributed considerably to the growth of
 electronics sector. The production in this sector has increased from Rs. 1,700 crores in 1992-93 to an estimated
 production figure of Rs.2,900 crores in tile terminal year of the VIII Plan i.e. 1996-97. Department of Electronics has
 been able to establish Some appropriate technologies in this area for various industry and service sectors. These are 200
 MWI200 KV HVDC systems, microprocessor based interlocking system for railway signalling, digital drive control
 system for railway signalling, digital drive control system for 5000 HP electric locomotives, transporter based Advanced
 Plant Automation and Control System, Computer Aided Factory Integration and Management system, etc.
 Demonstration projects in the area of Distribution Automation for tile power sector have also bee initiated in this period.
16. Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification Programme (STQC) is the major infrastructure of Department
 of Electronics (DoE) set up with the objective of assisting the Indian Electronics industry in improving the Quality and
 Reliability of electronic products, 10 that they can compete globally. The STQC programme has been in existence since
 1977, and was conceived on the recommendations of Bhabha Committee. The present status of STQC Directorate is
 "Attached Office" under Department of Electronics, Government of India.
16.1 STQC Directorate has established 21 laboratories (13 labs as Subordinate offices of DoE/DTQC and 8 labs
 under the control of the State Government). STQC has emerged as a strong certification body. STQC's certification
 schemes (SQ and S mark schemes) have been accredited by RV A, Netherlands-international accreditation body for
 accreditation of certification bodies.
16.2 Seventy industries certified under Quality management System viz., SQ (ISO 9(00) Scheme, thirteen industries
 certified under safety ('S' Mark), twenty-four Industries certified under IECQ (component Certification system) and one
 industry certified under EMC compliance (EMC mark). ISO 9000 Certification has been expanded to cover other
 technical areas in addition to electronics.
16.3 STQC has developed its own assessor resources comprising more than 50 Qualified Auditors, 8 Certified
 Quality Analysts, 4 Tick IT Qualified Auditors and 5 SEI Assessors located at STQC labs and Certification group of
 STQC Headquarters.
16.4 STQC Successfully implemented Indo-German technical co-operation project 'Quality improvement of India
 Electronic Products' covering Hardware and Software support in 11 topical areas at 10 STQC laboratories. With the
 success of the above project, STQC has initiated another project with German assistance, viz., Basic and Further
 Training of Experts in the field of Test Engineering and Quality Assurance in Electronics.
17. The Committee was informed that Electronics research and development in the country is persued through the

COMMITTEE ON SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

 various laboratories under Department of Space, Department of Atomic Energy, Department of Electronics, Department
 of Defence (R&D), Department of Telecommunications, Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, IITs and other
 academic institutions. Besides, some of die production agencies have strong in-house R&D base. The technology
 development is also carried out in major public undertakings and private industries as part of in-house development.
 Under the Department of Electronics a 1l\llOber of R&D projects have been initiated for technology development
 through Technology Development Council (TOC), the National Radar Council (NRC), the National Electronics Council
 (NMC), Electronics Material Development Council (EMDC), and National Photonics Council (NPC). Time-bound
 projects are implemented through separate scientific societies like Centre for Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Society
 for applied Microwave Electronics Engineering and Research (SAMEER), etc. Stage-I of the National High Voltage
 Direct Current (HVDCP) project is already over and Stage- II is in the progress. Other projects like Fibre-Optics. System
 Development, Advanced Technology Programme on computer Networking (ERNET), development of Higher Power
 Devices, etc. are making satisfactory progress. In order to encourage application-oriented research, design and
 development, the Electronics Research and Development Centres (EROCs) have been strengthened. These projects
 contribute towards establishment of a technology based and generating trained manpower in advanced technology areas.
17.1 The Committee was further wormed that in order to coordinate the efforts of various
 Departments/Organisations towards R&D in Electronics and to implement a synergistic programme in this regard,
 Department of Electronics proposes to set up Electronics R&D Coordination Council (ER&DCC). The Council would
 also act as an organ of Science Advisory Council (SAC) of the Cabinet for implementation, evaluation and feedback on
 policies and initiatives of SAC in respect of Electronics as well as provide an interface with the industry.
RECOMMENDATIONS
18. The Committee feels that the information technology has come to playa key role 10 the industrial
 transformation all over tile world. There is, therefore, a need to exploit fully the benefit of this technology. The
 Committee feels the need to set up an "PO level national information infrastructure which can_ coordinate with the
 various Ministries like Department of Telecommunications (Dot), Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, Ministry  of
 Human Resource Development and others 10 that a time-bound programme can be chalked out for the development
 and exploitation of this potential. The Committee further recommends that the Electronics and Information Technology
 Industry should be classified as a basic growth "infrastructure" industry which should enjoy  all the fiscal incentives
 available to the power and ~ sectors so that the technology Is within the reach of common man.
19. The Committee recommends that tile Department of Electronics should identify Joint R&D projects with other
 countries based on  mutual strength to participate 10 RAD on global  basis. Special efforts should he made to initiate
 technology development leading to more exports and development of Infrastructure to help boost the exports.
 Accordingly, R&D In few selected areas should be pursued keeping in view the high rate of obsolescence In electronics,
 the strategic need for making optimal use of national resources in order to derive the total benefit for the country. The
 Committee feels that the up of Electronics Research and Development Coordination Council (ER&DCC) is a welcome
 step as this would facilitate commercial exploitation of technologies with close interlace with the Industry.
19.1. At the same  time the Committee  feels the  need for substantial investment in the development of Human
 Resources in  view of our global Image In the area of software development.
20. In order to improve quality of and gain international recognition  for Indian products. The Committee
 recommends that the Department  should develop STQC as resource organisation for Quality Cel1iftcation In
 International activities. The present services of ITQC should be expanded to cover related areas such as
 environmental/energy management systems, energy auditing IT and telecommunication sectors.
21. The  Committee Is of the view  that National Testing and Calibration facility be created for process control
 automation components like actuators, transmitters and  sensors. An independent facility which can help control
 automation systems both with regard to hardware and software particularly of special applications is a must and could
 be set up on advanced lines.
22. The Committee observes that the use of internet facilities has been increasing worldwide.
The Committee has  been given to understand  that the number of  internet users in the world is of the order of 100
 million because the  facility  has come to be known as most effective medium for high speed  interphase particularly for
 accessing critical  data 8Dd communicating with others  users. In India the Viclesh Sanehar Nipm Ltd. (VSNL) is both
 the regulator as well as the service provider for  about 30,000 users of internet. At the lI8IJIe time, there are three other
 registered  service providers namely ERNET for educational  research, Software Technology Parks and National
 Information Centre essentially for Government departments. However, many internet users or potential users would

25.1 The Committee sees justification in the hike in plan allocation for rehabilitation of Semi-Conductor Complex
 Ltd. which had been destroyed due to fire a few years ago.

25.3 During the year, the operations of the Company were in the field of manufacturing pentium series of computers
 for marketing to the Government sector, packaged software and computer peripherals, networking, UNIX and Windows
 Platforms, consumer electronics such as CIV and B&W TV sets, electronics test and measuring instruments and
 computer education.
25.4 The Committee sees potential for the corporation and feels if sincereattempts are made to revive it, it can turn
 the comer. The Committee, . therefore, recommends that a suitable ad viable  package be worked out for its revival.. In
 that light, it Justifies the hike in the Budgetary support given to the Corporation.
26. The Committee finds that in the ease of Semi-Conductor Complex Ltd. located at Mohali a meagre allocation of

 completing the project during 1997-98 as per the approved revised cost estimates. The Committee has been given to

 Asian countries, where electronics sector II growing rapidly, mega fabrication facilities have been set-up or are in the

 major role in the development of the components sector. It therefore recommends that the requirement of funds of

27. In the representation submitted by the Electronic Component Industries Association (ELCINA), New-Delhi, it

---------------------            R E P O R T 
General Background 
Biotechnology aims at harnessing genetic diversity in the living organisms and uses advances in
cell and tissue culture, fermentation, enzy mology, immunology and recombinant DNA techniques.
Recombinant DNA techniques enable  genes to be transferred betw een organisms to produce desired
proteins of plant and animal origin as also human growth factors and hormones. It is one of the frontie r
areas of science. There have been many advances in this fiel d during the last forty years and the
developments in this fi eld have been particularly specta cular during the past fifteen years.
Biotechnology includes techniques which use living organisms or subs tances and from these organisms,
make or modify products to impr ove plants and animal  systems or develop other commercial and
industrial outputs. Researches conduc ted in the field of biotechnology have become very significant
because through the applications of  biotechnology, new approaches are being explored to solve various
problems faced by society. It has application in agriculture, he alth and industr y. Many chemical
approaches, currently in use may, in course of time, be replaced by biological techniques where wor k
can be accomplished at low temperatures and pressures with lower energy inputs. This branch of science
has the potential of generating jobs, creating value-added produc ts and employing women and weake r
section of the society in  a cleaner environment. Biotechnology can also ensure sustainable development
by regenerating the degraded environment. 
2.         An integrated programme was launc hed for the development of  biotechnology in 1986 when a
separate Department of Biot echnology was set up. Earlier the National Biotechnology Board was
coordinating the activi ties in this field. This was set .up in 1982 under the Ministry of Science and
Technology pursuant to the recommendation of the then Science Advisory Committee to the Cabinet. At
present the Department of Biot echnology offers' support t6 R&D and manufacture, identifies and
establishes centres of excellence for R&D, promotes large scale use of biotechnology, evolves integrated
programme for manpower development,  establishes infrastructural faci lities to support R&D as well as
production, evolves safety guidelines, promotes university-industry interaction, serves as nodal point for 
specific international collaboration, looks af ter the manufacture and application of cell- based vaccines 
and coordinates the activities of the National Institute of Immunology (NII) and the National Facility for
Animal Tissue and Cell Culture (NFATCC), which are two autonomous institutions working in the field
of biotechnology. The De partment also remains in  constant touch with th e International Centre fo r
Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB). 
3.         In order to assess whether the Depa rtment of Biotechnology is fulfilling its mandate, the
committee decided to study the working of the Depa rtment on the basis of the Annual Report for the
year 1992-93. 
4.         The Committee was apprised of the various activities of the, Department, its thrust areas, etc. by
the Secretary and other of ficers of the Department . The committee was informed that the Department
has two advisory committees, name ly, the Scientific Advisory Co mmittee-DBT (SAC-DBT) and the 
Standing Advisor y Committee-Overseas (SAC-O) to provide new directions, define policy issues,

monitoring of various programmes and identificati on of new areas for R&D. The Department has
established a strong infra structure for biotechnology research and services in various national
laboratories and academic institutions. Manpower training at various  levels and R&D programmes have
been supported from the viewpoint of attaining excellence and for developing products and processes

development and demonstration. The Department has given special emphasis on demonstration
pr0grammes to benefit the farmers and the rural population. Some of these programmes relate to oil
plam, biological pest control, bi ofertilizers, aquacultur e, embryo transfer technology, sericulture and
leather biotechnology. Cattle herd  improvement using embryo tran sfer technology, development and
production of immunodiagnostic  kits and immunologica l approaches to fert ility control are S&T
projects in mission mode which are being efficiently implemented by the Department. 
5.         The 13 Task Forces comprising experts from all over the country have prepared a R&D profile
for the next 5 years and R&D support would be provi ded in areas leading to product development an e
excellence in research. 
Biofertilizers and Biological Insect Control Programme 
6.         The Committee felt that some of the achievements of the Department of Biotechnology have not
reached the common man in our country. In this regard, the committee quoted the example o f
biofertilizers, bioinsecticides and biopesticides. The Commi ttee was of the view th at blue green algae
and rhizobium are not very much in usage, though it has been claimed by the Department that the use o f
biofertilizers would lead to higher yields. The Committee also wanted to know whether there was any
programme with the Department to popularise the use of biofertilizers in the country. In view of the cost
effectiveness of biofertiliz ers and also due to the fact that biof ertilizers do not advers ely affect the soil
like the chemical fertili zers, the Committee wanted to know about  the steps taken by the Department to
promote the use of biofertilizers. 
7.         The representatives of the Department  clarified that the Depart ment of Biotechnology has
launched a Technology Development and Demonstration Programme in  1990. It has a limited objective
of improvement of the quality of biofertilizers by making use of modern, biotechnological methods
bringing out quality contro l aspects and also ensuring a feedback  from the farmers to  the laboratory so
that there could be consta nt improvement in areas lif e enhancing the shelf-life of the biofer tilizers. At 
present the States covered are Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jammu and Kashmir, Gujarat, Madhya
Pradesh, Kerala and Punjab. In the eastern region in West Bengal in Sundarbans a major programme
was taken up on the use of blue green algae in th e marshy areas. According to the State Agricultural
Department, there was 7 per cent ri se in the yield of rice after its use in limited field trial. The
production of blue green algae was 200 tonnes in the country in  1992 through the 60 sub-centres of the 
Ministry of Agriculture. The estimated demand for th e blue green algae is cons iderable because there is
going to be 40 million hectares under rice cultivation and scientists feel that  out of the 40 million
hectares at least 15 million hect ares should be supplied with blue  green algae as a supplement to
chemical fertilizers. Th e production of rhizobium is 1,000 tonnes from 70 centres of the Ministry o f
Agriculture As regard comparative studies about th e use of chemical fertil izers and supplementing it
with biofertilizers like blue gr een algae, these studies have b een taken up by the Department o f
Biotechnology in its various centres. It has been clearly noticed that  chemical fertilizers in some of the
areas have reduced the soil fertility to a considerable extent. By supplementing Chemical-fertilizers with 
biofertilizers, the yield per hect are has increased and the plants look greener and hormones are also
produced. It also results in a sa ving of 25% of Nitrogen. The repres entatives of the Department also
informed the Committee that the Department is tr ying to mix biofertilizers by combining blue green
algae, rhizobium, with mycorrhiza and this mixture is working well. These e xperiments may eventually
lead to the modifying of the ratio of the use of biofertilizers and chemical fertilizers.
