INTRODUCTION
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Ninety-third Report on the
 Action Taken by the Department of Biotechnology on the recommendations contained in the Eighty-seventh Report of the
 Committee on Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Biotechnology.
 
            The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Biotechnology on the recommendations
 contained in the Eighty-seventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Biotechnology which was presented to the
 Rajya Sabha on 18
th April, 2001.
 
            There are sixteen recommendations contained in the Eighty-seventh Report of the Committee.  Action Taken Notes on the
 recommendations of the Committee, were received from the Department on 23rd July, 2001.
 
            In the meeting held on 28 th November, 2001 the Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report and adopted the
 same.
 
 
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                       C. RAMACHANDRAIAH
November 28, 2001                                                                                                   Chairman,
   Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology ,Environment & Forests.        
 
 
 
R E P O R T
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Biotechnology on the
 recommendations contained in the Eighty-Seventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of
 Biotechnology which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 18th April, 2001 and laid on the Lok Sabha on the 18 th April,
 2001.  There are sixteen recommendations contained in the eighty-Seventh Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes
 on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 23rd July, 2001.
 
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by
 the Department of Biotechnology are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that it is not opposed to enhanced allocations to the Department. While it is necessary
 that the Department keeps itself posted with the developments abroad in the field of biotechnology, it should
 choose projects with utmost caution with a view to ensure that they are in the best interests of the country.
                 
(Para 10)
 
Action Taken by the Department

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/93rd.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:29]
 
The Department has been from the very beginning interacting with all the concerned scientific agencies, user
 Ministries/Departments, national laboratories, universities, state level institutions and NGOs to identify and prioritize
 programmes considering needs and interests of the country. The department is advised by a Scientific Advisory
 Committee. There is also a Standing Advisory Committee (Overseas), a novel feature of this department with non-resident
 Indian scientists as its members to give advice and inputs on the developments abroad in the field of biotechnology. The
 Biotechnology Research and Promotion Committee (BRPC), a High Powered Committee of inter-disciplinary experts and
 16 subject specific Task Forces are also operational to identify, recommend, review and monitor projects in the best
 interest of the country. Every effort has been made to keep itself abreast with latest development world over.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply and commends the efforts being made by the Department in
 involving non-resident Indians in its programmes.
 
Recommendation
 
As regards the programmes under the forest trees the same need to be developed extensively with a view to
 increase the forest cover. This, in turn, would help in arresting ecological imbalances. Besides, the technology be
 made available for social forestry programmes.                 
       
(Para 17)
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department has a major programme on forest tree improvement. Tissue culture regeneration protocols have been
 standardized for a large number of economically important tree species and these are now being adopted for large scale
 multiplication. The tissue culture pilot plants set up by the Department at Tata Energy Research Institute, New Delhi and
 National Chemical Laboratory, Pune which were later converted to Micro propagation Technology Parks are producing
 large quantities of elite planting material of forest trees. Approx. 70 lakhs plants have been produced so far and field
 planted over an area of 8000 ha. at multi- locations in 17 states across the country.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply. However, it would like the Department to focus on the States facing problems of
 deforestation or environmental degradation in any other form.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee is constrained to observe that the leprosy vaccine developed by the National Institute of
 Immunology is yet to be included by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare in its leprosy control programme.
 The Committee has been given to understand that voluntary agencies have made use of 24 lakhs doses of the
 vaccines whereas the Ministry of Health continues to import the vaccines instead of making use of the one
 developed by the National Institute of Immunology. If it is really so, the Committee observes that it constitutes
 draining out of the precious foreign exchange from the national exchequer. This needs to be pursued with the
 Ministry of Health on priority basis.
 
                                                                                                                        (Para 19)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department has already approached Ministry of Health & Family Welfare at the highest level with the request
 to make use of, LAPROVAC in the National Leprosy Eradication Programme, as a therapeutic immunomodulator.
 

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/93rd.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:29]
Comments
 
            The Committee notes with concern that the outcome of the efforts made at the highest level with the
 Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to make use of LAPROVAC in the National Leprosy Eradication
 Programme has not been indicated.  The Committee apprehends that the Department has either not succeeded in
 persuading the Ministry of Health to make use of LAPROVAC or something is amiss that Ministry of Health finds
 it difficult to make use of indigenous supplies of LAPROVAC.  The Committee would like the Department to take
 up the matter again with the Ministry of Health again and, if necessary, approach the Cabinet Secretariat for
 advice or for placing the matter before the Cabinet.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee commends the work done by the Department in the field of rice genome sequencing and observes that more
 such programmes need to be undertaken especially in crops like pulses which are in short supply in the country, maize, oilseeds,
 and other dry farming crops keeping in view the extremely varied climate, cropping patterns, variety of crops available in the
 country.
                                                                                                 (Para 22)  
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Rice Genome is the smallest of the most economically important cereals like wheat, barley, maize and
 sorghum. There is considerable conservation of gene order among these genomes and hence the information gained from
 rice will be helpful in understanding other cereal genomes. The outcome of sequencing  programme would be
 identification of many genes of interest particularly yield component, plant architecture, resistance to stresses and pests,
 diseases, drought, salinity etc.
 
So far as legumes are concerned, functional genomics of chickpea has received high priority at National Centre for
 Plant Genome Research (NCPGR), New Delhi. The EST, sequences, characterization of putative chickpea disease
 resistant gene and cloning of molecular markers associated with plant differentiation are the ongoing activities. The
 Department at the moment does not have any programme on genomics of maize. However' it is intended to have a
 collaborative programme with CIMMYT, Mexico - the applied Biotechnological Centre which is working on molecular
 markers, genetic engineering and apomixis of maize.
 
In the area of wheat genomics, one of the Department supported Centres has recently become a member of
 International Wheat Microsatellite Consortium (IWMC). This initiative has received positive response from the other
 members of IWMC.
 
Comments
 
The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in the field of Rice and wheat genomics.  The
 Committee observes that the Department should continue to explore more areas of Genetic Engineering in
 furthering the research.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee has perused the information available in respect of Patent Cell over the internet. While all the
 institutions etc. can be accessed and through them the homepage of the Department, the home page is not directly
 accessible for some reason of confidentiality attached to it or because of some technical reasons. This needs to be
 looked into. The Committee is also of the view that the efforts be made to make the scientists aware of the need for
 taking patents and procedures for applying a patent must be simplified and displayed over the Internet along with
 facility for downloading of forms as far as possible. The information about the patents applied must also be made
 available which is perhaps not available at present.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 25)

Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department has easily and directly accessible website over the internet. Apart from all the relevant information
 about Department, it contains the format of the application for patent filing both in pdf and html. formats. The hard copy
 of the format is circulated to interested organizations, as and when they require and for reference in their libraries. To
 encourage scientists to patent their innovations and create awareness on the procedures four National Roving seminars
 and an equal number of lectures were organized in the last two years. Two publications brought out for this purpose have
 been widely circulated. A simplified and supportive system is already in place to facilitate patenting. The information
 regarding the patents applied cannot be made available on the internet for the reasons of confidentiality. The Department
 is having bilingual (English and Hindi) website with the addresses www.dbtindia.nic.in
 and www.dbtindia.org
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply and would like to point out that the Committee has not at all questioned the
 confidentiality about the patents applied or otherwise.  What was pointed out is that the homepage of the website
 should be easily accessible.  If this too is confidential then there is no point in having any website whatsoever.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that efforts be made for developing cheaper technologies in waste treatment to enable
 industries to readily accept and install the same. As oil spill/sludge has become an important cause of pollution in
 the high seas in the recent years and is liable to affect the marine life, Oil Zapper could be marketed worldwide to
 contain oil spills.
                                                                                                                                            
 (Para 27)
Action Taken by the Department
 
Oilzapper technology developed by Tata Energy Research institute (TERI), New Delhi has already been transferred
 to Sriram Biotech Ltd. Hyderabad and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (BPCL), Mumbai. Sriram Biotech Ltd. is
 already supplying oilzapper within the country. In addition, these companies have received requests from Pakistan, Saudi
 Arabia, Philippines, Malaysia which are being negotiated. Further, cost effective technologies for ecorestoration of mine
 dumps, starch factory waste water treatment, dye industry effluent treatment, desulphurisation of biogas have been
 developed and demonstrated to user industries.
 
Comments
 
            The Committee notes with satisfaction the efforts made by the Department. 
Recommendation
The Committee commends the progress made in the field of vaccine development specially the edible vaccines. 
 The Department should endeavour to pass on these technologies to industry for marketing purposes. The
 Committee observes the need to develop more such vaccines for diseases like Hepatitis B virus, Hepatitis E virus
 that are highly infectious.
                                                                                                                                  (Para 30)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department has already taken action to expand the programme on edible vaccines so as to include important
 vaccines for several infectious diseases. As and when technology is ready for transfer to the industry, appropriate action
 will be taken.
 
Comments

Recommendation
 
While the Committee is satisfied with the programme related to setting up of Biotechnology Parks, it
 emphasizes the need for such Parks if they help the cause of the development of wasteland in villages which could
 possibly be another area of augmenting the income of farmers/women in rural areas.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 32)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
Several projects are operational for the development of wasteland in villages for economic benefit to the farmers
 and women in rural areas. The Department is framing more programmes/schemes for the benefit of the farmers, women
 and weaker sections of the society, keeping in view their location specific problems and circumstances.    As and when the
 proposals will be received from the State Governments and other organizations, emphasis will be given on these
 recommendations.
 
Comments
 
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
 
The Committee commends the concept of Biovillage taken up by the Department. The Committee however feels the
 need for more such projects being undertaken in those villages where chemical fertilizer is abundantly used. Training also
 needs to be provided for use of the bio-fertilizers in view of their minimal impact on environment.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 34)
Action Taken by the Department
 
Training and use of biofertilizers is an integral part of Biovillege project. Programmes are implemented in Madhya
 Pradesh and West Bengal. A network project on Integrated Nutrient Management has also been implemented at 7 centres
 based on important cropping patterns of the country. Through this initiative, various packages have been developed for
 effective use of biofertilizers, resulting in reduction of chemical fertilizer consumption.
 
Comments
 
            The Committee notes the reply.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee feels that the country must aim to regain its lost glory in silk trade as it has the advantage of
 production of all four own commercial silk varieties viz; mulberry, tusser, eri and muga. As sericulture is suitable
 for marginal, small and landless farmers, it has tremendous scope for expansion in view of its employment
 generation potential. Efforts should therefore be made to strengthen the linkages between extension and R&D
 units. The technology delivery systems should be streamlined by providing need based training and effective field
 demonstrations by using various communication methods.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 36)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department is working closely with the Central Silk Board (CSB)- the user agency for sericulture from
 identification of R&D programmes to their implementation. The department is providing R&D inputs to CSB. Further

 extension work is being done by CSB through their units. For example; demonstration of Integrated Pest Management
 (IPM) package for control of uzifly- a serious pest of silkworm, artificial semi-synthetic diets for rearing of silkworm
 diseases and utilizing DNA markers for improvement of breeds through breeding programmes etc.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that India is one of the first countries in the world to initiate a Bioinformatics
 programme. Besides, given the advantages the country has in IT sector and its expertise in mathematics and high
 knowledge base, special emphasis needs to be given to this aspect as sustainability and dissemination of the data is
 necessary for the success of plans. The researchers should also have the access to updated knowledge to keep
 themselves abreast of research elsewhere in the world. This would help avoid duplicating the research and in
 patenting the research already conducted.
                                                                                                                    (Para 38)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The department has so far established 55 Bioinformates Centre spread across all over the country with necessary
 computer and communication infrastructure and sufficient manpower to handle the IT applications in the area of
 Biotechnology and modern Biology. These centre are well equipped to collect, analyse and disseminate information
 recourses to researchers both from national and international information sources. The department also provides support
 to R&D activities  in Bioinformatics to utilise the expertise available from the IT sector towards development of software
 packages and other tools for bioinformatics and biotechnology applications.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply but it would like the Department to continue efforts aimed at providing the
 latest information in relevant fields to help researchers.
 
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that studies conducted under the bilateral cooperation should aim at research in
 developing drugs for diseases that are particular to our country such as Kala-azar, plague, tuberculosis & malaria
 etc.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 41)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The efforts have been made under the bilateral /multilateral cooperation to collaborate in tropical diseases prevalent
 in India and the region. Under bilateral collaboration with Sri Lanka malaria is an area of priority research. Under INDO-
US Vaccine Action Programme vaccines and diagnostics are targeted towards major tropical diseases like tuberculosis,
 malaria, HIV, hepatitis virus, laishmaniasis etc.
 
Comments
 
            The Committee notes with satisfaction the efforts made by the Department and hopes that more and more
 countries would be invited to join bilateral/multilateral cooperation to fight the menace of the diseases affecting the
 region.

Recommendation
The Committee expresses its satisfaction with the work being done by the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and
 Diagnostics (CDFD) in the field of Automated Genome Analysis,  Bioinformatics   Diagnostics,   DNA
 Fingerprinting, Instrumentation and Research in, among other areas, cancer biology, computational biology and
 Immunology etc. The Committee however feels that the country's population having touched 1020 million and as
 the crimes, conflicts and paternity disputes are expected to arise with more frequency with the rising pace of
 population, it was time to consider whether there was need to set up full fledged institutes to provide the services to
 the institutions and people expeditiously and with minimum of costs.
                                                                                                                        (Para 45 & 46)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The Department envisages CDFD to become a referral centre for DNA fingerprinting activities. It is expected that
 the institute will provide guide to other DNA fingerprinting laboratories. An Advisory Committee is being set up to assess
 the requirement of DNA fingerprinting, profiling and diagnostic activities.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
The Committee commends the progress made by BIBCOL from a company facing financial crunch to revenue
 generating one. The Committee is happy to note that it is able to sustain its regular activities. The Committee
 reiterates its earlier recommendation that efforts must be made to produce new & improved vaccines and
 immunodiagnostics such as rabies measles, recombinant Hepatitis 'B' vaccine, etc.
                                                                                                                                            (Para 53)
 
Action Taken by the Department
 
The company has been registered under Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). The BIFR has
 appointed IDBI as Operating Agency to prepare the revival scheme of the company. The Operating Agency submitted
 financial restructuring and product diversification plan to BIFR. Action will be taken on this as and when the BIFR and
 Govt. approve.
 
Comments
 
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
 
The Committee observes that as the programmes of the Department are liable to benefit different sections of the
 society, the Department must take initiative to approach Doordarshan for at least a few minutes slot to disseminate
 information on at least one programme every day in a bid to reach the sections of the society for whom it was meant.
                                                                                                                                    (Para 54)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department has taken initiative for dissemination of information of its programmes and schemes over
 Doordarshan in its Turning Point and Gyan Darshan sections. The Department will make all efforts for giving wide
 publicity over Doordarshan. A major programme on popularization of biotechnology has been formulated for
 implementation.

 Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendation
      The Committee commends the steps being taken by the Department in augmenting its scientific and industrial
 capabilities towards the economic and social development of the Country.  The Committee however recommends that
 besides the on-going research projects, the Department should also support employment generating research such as
 research on Bamboo from which millions of people earn their livelihood worldwide.  This would help in generating
 employment among rural people.
(Para 10)
Action Taken by the Department
      The Steering Committee for formulation of Tenth Five Year Plan on S&T has assigned to the Department of Science &
 Technology the formulation of the mission on Bamboo.  CSIR would provide the requisite inputs for the mission.
Comments
            While the Committee notes the reply with satisfaction, it would like the Department to identify more of such
 projects which can generate employment without any investment on the part of the rural folk and thus help them

 endeavour to bring about diversification in R&D work.  While the user services for the industry may continue to
 be provided, prioritization and diversification of research may help decrease the dependence on non-plan
 expenditure.  Efforts should also be made to secure research work from abroad to the extent possible.

Recommendation
            The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in 73
rd report and observes that there is a need
 to progressively modernise the CSIR Laboratories.  The Committee observes that the process of modernisation
 should be time bound.  The Department should also spell out precisely the areas of modernisation being
 undertaken/ proposed to be undertaken in the laboratories.  The Department should also ensure that the
 modernisation matches the international standards.  Also, the Committee should be apprised about the training

 the end of the current financial year, this phase is expected to be over.  CSIR is seized with the matter of modernisation to
 continue and as recommended by the Committee, the next phase of modernisation proposed for the Tenth Five Year Plan
 relates to Infrastructure Renovation and Refurbishment.

 brought about in the laboratories, giving details laboratory-wise so that the Committee could consider visiting any
 of these laboratories during its visit to those areas.  The Committee would also like the modernisation to be made
 an integral part of each of the laboratories notwithstanding the phases of recession like the one through which the
 Indian economy, like many other countries of the world, is passing through.
 
NATIONAL S&T HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT
Recommendation
            The Committee observes that the Universities and Institutions will have to play a meaningful role to achieve
 widespread excellence in both teaching quality and high calibre human resources.  Therefore, there is a need for
 reviewing and strengthening/revamping the existing S&T supports systems in the universities and other
 educational institutions, be it in terms of infrastructure or quantum of funding as well as operational structures
 and mechanisms.  The issues related to the institutional mechanisms, policy guidelines, approval and clearance of
 procedures should be looked into with a view to simplify and make them user friendly.
(Para 26)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Scientific Advisory Committee to the Cabinet is seized with the matter of creating suitable mechanisms and
 policy directions to bring in together Universities/Institutions and S&T support systems for developing high calibre
 human resources.  The Steering Committee on Science & Technology for the Tenth Five Year Plan inter alia has also
 dwelt on the issue on interface between industry, R&D institutions and academia for S&T.  The recommendations of the
 Steering Committee are to be submitted to Planning Commission, which in turn, is expected to appropriately reflect the
 issues in its Report on Tenth Five Year Plan.
Comments
            The Committee notes the position.

            The Committee feels that CSIR should also consider introducing Scientific Research Scholarships to school

CSIR has already initiated a scheme known as CSIR Programme for Youth Leadership in Science (CPYLS)

 the CSIR laboratory.  Those students passing XII class exam with 90% marks in science are further encouraged to pursue
 science at degree level by giving them the opportunity to work for 14 weeks/year for three years in any of the CSIR labs
 during vacations.  They are called ‘CSIR Students Associate’ and are given a stipend of Rs.500/- a week.  These Students
 Associates would also be provided support to pursue M.Sc.

 introduced special awards for women scientists.

 observations of the students already availing the benefit of such schemes be obtained in writing/through their
 reactions and be made the basis/background of Newspapers/Electronic media ads with new visuals, pictures
 delivering messages.  This would help attract more students.

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT BY INDUSTRY (RDI)
Recommendation
            The Committee observes that the socio-economic advancement of a nation demands a strong relationship
 between Industry and R&D laboratories, which unfortunately is not a reality in India.  Rather the wholesome
 involvement of national R&D with industry, which is a hallmark of the advanced industrial societies, is missing in
 India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that CSIR laboratories should put more emphasis  on  consolidating
its partnership with the industry so that the technologies developed by the laboratories can be commercialised and
 fully exploited.  More the commercialisation of technologies, more would be the confidence in the CSIR
 laboratories, providing further impetus to their R&D activities.
(Para 35)
Action Taken by the Department
            The CSIR is fully cognizant of the Committee’s concerns, however mere responsiveness of the CSIR and R&D is
 not enough.  The state of health and well being of the industry and conducive and enabling environment are needed for
 symbiosis of national R&D with industry.  These aspects of the innovation system are to be developed concurrently,
 which are beyond the ken of CSIR.  Nonetheless CSIR is making vigorous efforts to bring about such a system.
Comments
            The Committee observes that what has been stated by the Department is indeed true.  It is more so in
 periods like the one through which Indian economy is at present passing through with slump in economic activity. 
 But even in present periods competitiveness, cost controls and product innovations could be of help.  The
 laboratories must endeavour to make inroads in the industry with such qualities which help improve quality, cut
 down costs and product innovations.

Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that the need for transfer of technology in bringing improvement  in industrial
 productivity can not be underestimated.  The Committee is pained to observe that Transfer of Technology
 programmes have moved at snail’s pace.  It is necessary to identify the prevailing constraints and have insight of
 Industrial sector problems and then devise appropriate technologies to address the problems.  To that end, the
 Committee recommends that a multi-disciplinary team should work on priority basis for identification and
 solution of the problems being faced with regard to the technology.

            The thrust of Committee’s observation is that it is necessary to identify & assess industrial sector’s problems and
 devise appropriate technologies to address the problems and evolve solutions through a multi-disciplinary team effort.

 institutions, related to their specific problems in technology absorption, adaptation, development and commercialization. 
 This is done through inter-departmental and inter disciplinary Committees such as Technology Advisory Committees and
 Project Review Committees.  The Department through its various plan schemes promotes close linkages between the
 industry and R&D system, so as to encourage formulation and implementation of activities & programmes which are
 mutually relevant and beneficial to industrial units as well as R&D laboratories.  CSIR laboratories have been directly
 involved in conducting industrial research and are therefore, in a position to identify problems of industry in their
 respective areas of operation and work towards finding solutions for the same.

            The Committee notes the reply.

FOOD AND FOOD PROCESSING
Recommendation
            The Committee visited Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysore a few years back
 and had the occasion to see some of the machines like large scale dosa making machine.  The Committee doubts
 whether there is demand for machines designed to cater large scale commercial requirement.  The Committee
 would therefore like to impress on all concerned to engage themselves in activities which are either against
 confirmed orders or can otherwise be gainfully exploited.
(Para 55)
Action Taken by the Department
            The Committee’s observations that activities should be taken up only which have either confirmed orders or can
 otherwise be gainfully exploited are well received. CFTRI efforts had always been to generate technologies that can be
 gainfully exploited, sometimes these are market led and sometimes lead the market. In respect of the dosa making
 machine CFTRI estimates the demand of 2000 numbers of dosa making machines, with 400 dosa per hour capacity, from
 large catering fast food establishments and social feeding centers.

            The Committee is not satisfied with the reply and feels that the recommendation made by the Committee
 was of general nature and was supported by an instance.  In case the recommendation was not based on just
 assumption, the facts in this regard should have been brought forward to clarify whether the instant case was

            The Committee feels that in order to provide impetus to the technologies developed by the CSIR

 State Governments to waive Sales & Trade tax so that optimum exploitation of technologies can be ensured.

R E P O R T
 
1.   The Chairman Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 referred*the Biological Diversity Bill, 2000**as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15th May, 2000 and pending therein to the Standing
 Committee on Science & Technology Environment & Forests for examination and report.
2.   At their first meeting held on 18 th July, 2000, the Committee held general discussion on the various provisions of the Bill and
 referred to the importance and urgency of the task before the Committee. The Committee had also the benefit of presentation on the
 subject by the Secretary and other Officers of the Ministry of Environment & Forests on the Bill under reference and the need to
 bring the proposed legislation. The Committee observed that the Bill dealt with an important issue and required a thorough study. 
 The Committee then considered its future course of action and decided that a press Communique might be issued in all the national
 dailies both in English and Hindi versions inviting therein memoranda on the subject matter of the Bill from the interested
 organizations/institutions/individuals having knowledge and expertise in the field or otherwise interested in the subject.  The
 Committee also desired that the contents of the Press Communique be given wide publicity through All India Radio and
 Doordarshan.  The Chairman also requested the Members to suggest the names of organisations, individuals, etc. from whom
 memoranda might be invited. Besides, the Committee directed the Secretariat to request the Ministry of Environment & Forests to
 forward to this Secretariat a list of Organizations/Experts/ Individuals in the field along with their complete addresses.  The
 Committee also desired that they might undertake an on-the-spot study visit to various parts of the country to elicit the views of the
 representatives of various organisations, associations and general public on the subject matter of   the Bill.
Accordingly, a press communiqué inviting memoranda etc.  was issued on 18
th August 2000.
As per decision taken by the Committee letters inviting Memoranda containing comments/suggestions on the provisions of the
 Bill were also issued to Organizations/Experts/ Individuals in the field whose names were furnished by the Ministry of Environment
 & Forests.
3.   In all 35 Memoranda containing comments/suggestions on the various provisions of the Bill were received by the Committee
 from various associations/organizations and individuals etc. which were sent to the Ministry of Environment & Forests for their
 Comments/observations (Annexure-II).
4.   Biodiversity or the variety of living organism is the foundation on which life on earth sustains itself. This variety among living

fdfdfdf
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/95threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:33]
 organisms extends to both variety within each species, between different species and ecosystems, which support them. Biodiversity
 is a fundamental necessity of nature to maintain the ecological balance on the planet. No single organism can exist on its own; each
 one depends on numerous others in myriad ways to sustain itself and its kind. This interdependence between organisms, often
 referred to as the web of life, is greatly endangered today as a result of our insensitive tampering with the nature's well-preserved
 checks and balances.
5.   Scientists and conservationists all over the world agree that life on Earth faces enormous risks due to rapid and large-scale loss of
 bio-diversity, unprecedented in the history of humankind.
______________________________________________________________________________
*    Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II dated the 28th June, 2000.
** Annexure-I
Moreover, diversity has an insurance value, for it widens the range of environmental conditions under which different species can
 perform key ecological and economic functions. India is endowed with a rich biodiversity, as the country is well spread out in a
 wide variety of climatic zones and habitats that range from tropical rainforests to alpine vegetation, and from temperate forests to
 coastal wetlands. Eastern Himalayas and Western Ghats are two of world's 18 biodiversity hotspots, where bulk of Earth's plants
 and animals are found. India is one of the twelve mega-biodiversity areas of the world with over 45,000 wild species of plants and
 77,000 wild species of animals on record.
6.   India's rich biodiversity that exists today is estimated to be the result of over three and half million years of evolution, which
 involved speciation, migration, plate tectonics, natural holocausts, extinction and of late the human influences, interventions and
 disturbances. But during the last century, biodiversity has been drastically falling due to indiscriminate rise in human activities in
 and around forests, wetlands, rivers and oceans.
7.   There are fewer varieties of wild plants and animals today than a few decades before, and the lost varieties are gone forever. A
 high degree of endemism makes the Indian biodiversity particularly vulnerable to extinction. In last few decades, at least 50 percent
 of India’s forests have been cut down, 70 percent of its water bodies have been polluted, its grasslands cultivated and its coasts
 degraded. In addition, hunting, overexploitation, poisoning by pesticides, excessive botanical and zoological collection,
 displacement by exotic varieties and a host of other activities have taken a heavy toll of biodiversity. Already, 23 species, which
 include cheetah, the lesser one-horned rhino, and pink-headed duck, have become extinct in India, and many more species of plants
 and animals might have vanished without anyone noticing them. Nearly 750 species of plants and animals appear to be on the verge
 of extinction and the Gangetic river dolphin, Red Panda, Lion tailed macaque and the Bengal tiger are some of the highly
 endangered animals in the country today.
8.   Indiscriminate and illegal trade in wild plants and animals, combined with ecologically insensitive development projects,
 explosive growth in human population and the resultant pressure on the natural resources, are the main reasons of chronic
 biodiversity loss in India during last few decades. Specific causes have always varied with ecosystems. Even after independence,
 forests continued to be plundered in the country on a large-scale by the industries in construction, furniture making, paper & pulp,
 mining and textiles, until very recently when most of the remaining forest cover in India has come under the protection of national
 parks and wildlife sanctuaries. An important cause of habitat destruction in the Eastern Himalayan states like Sikkim and Arunachal
 Pradesh is jhum, or shifting cultivation, which is practised in 70% of the land in the region. Some experts believe that given
 sufficient area to operate, and long enough fallow periods, jhum cultivation can be sustainable. However, population pressures have
 led to a shortening of the fallow cycle, which has made this form of cultivation totally unsustainable. The Forest Survey of India has
 recently estimated that 57% of the forests have been lost due to shifting cultivation.
9.   Human interference has intensified a natural process like siltation to a degree where it has become a major threat to the wetlands
 in India. The Dal lake receives 80 000 tonnes of silt from Talbal Nalla every year, while the Chilka lake has been shrinking by
 roughly 1.5 square kilometres every year since 1925 because of siltation and the reclamation of marginal areas. Another process
 affecting wetlands is eutrophication the process by which a body of water becomes either naturally or by pollution, rich in dissolved
 nutrients and often shallow with a seasonal deficiency in dissolved oxygen.  Chilika lake in Orissa, for instance, is infested  with the
 weed Potamogeton pectinatus as a result of eutrophication of its water from the fertilizer run-offs regularly flowing in from the
 surrounding farmlands. Further, intensive fishing in rivers, lakes and seas can reduce fish populations to such an extent that they are
 no longer able to regenerate a viable number for their continued survival. The best example of this is the whale shark, which is now
 being mercilessly caught in most coastal regions of India for both eating and its fins, which command a huge price in the
 international markets.
10.  Biodiversity is India's real wealth and its resource base determines and ensures this country's survival and growth. Therefore,
 conserving and protecting this natural endowment is our primary necessity. Historically, our culture and civilization evolved and
 edified around this immense natural wealth. Our present population, with nearly 80% still directly dependent on agriculture and
 forests, cannot afford to be different.

“Commercial utilization means end uses of biological researches for commercial utilization such as drug, industrial enzymes,

12.  Dr. Ranjitsinh of Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH), New Delhi in his presentation on 19 th June

 decide in consultation with the Biodiversity Management Committee (BMC) created by local bodies i.e. panchayats, municipalities

 sustainable use of biodiversity and whether it would be able to enforce that sustainable use and in the process forego revenue and
 also earn the ire of their own people who would be out to exploit the biological resources for not just personal bonafide use but for
 commercial purposes?  If not, what could be the safeguards?  “Sustainable use” means the use of biological resources after
 ascertaining on a scientific basis the harvestable   surplus of   biological   resources  in  a   given  ecosystem  after  ensuring  that  
 the productivity and ecological security of the said ecosystem, biome and biological resources were maintainable at the optimum
 level on a long term basis and also ensure that in the harvesting and removal of such harvestable surplus no adverse impact was
 caused on other biota or the land in terms of Clause 7 of the Bill.  He submitted before the Committee that it should be omitted.  It

 hardship and corruption. 
13.  Arya Vaidya Sala, Kottakkal, Kerala made following suggestions for consideration of the Committee that Clauses 7, 8, 17, 18,

14.  All India Biotech Association, New Delhi made following suggestions for consideration of the Committee:-
(i)         The proposed Bill should concentrate on Sustainable Use of Biological Resources and formulate the policy for

 replenishment of Biological Resources could be administered by the NBA.
(ii)        Reaffirming the ownership of the entire Nation as such over the Biological Resources, Equitable Sharing of Benefits
 should be restricted only to royalty payments for commercialisation of Biological Resources.
(iii)       Proposals for transfer of technology and joint ownership and relocation of production facilities should be dropped.
(iv)       The Biotech industry be granted representation in the NBA and the State Biodiversity Board.
(v)        No prior approvals should be required to be taken for commercialisation of a Biological Resource.  In the present
 competitive scenario confidentiality of research and development should be granted highest priority.
(vi)       NBA should be empowered to sponsor scientists for generating intellectual wealth from the Biological Resources
 and create healthy competition for research and development.
(vii)      While fixing rates of royalties, due consideration should be given to R&D efforts put in by various commercial
 players in developing a commercial product from the Biological Resources.  This would avoid the cascading of
 costs making the end products out of reach of the common man.
(viii)      Companies with minority foreign equity or foreign management should be treated as Indian Companies under the
 Bill.  This is essential to ensure technical advancement of the country, which could then be used for commercial

15.  The Committee undertook study visits to Bangalore, Goa, Pune, Mumbai, Ahmedabad from 15

A
BILL
To   provide    for   conservation  of  Biological  Diversity,  sustainable use  of   
      its  components  and  equitable sharing   of   the  benefits  arising   out  of      
     the   use  of  biological resources and  for matters connected  therewith or  
    incidental  thereto.
 
        WHEREAS India is rich in biological diversity and associated traditional and contemporary
 knowledge system relating thereto;
AND WHEREAS India is a party of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity
 signed at Rio de Janeiro on the 5th day of June 1992;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention came into force on the                   29 th December, 1993;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention reaffirms the sovereign rights of the State over their
 biological resources;
AND W HEREAS the said Convention has the main objective of conservation of biological
 diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising
 out of utilization of genetic resources;
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to provide for conservation, sustainable utilization
 and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of utilization of genetic resources and also to give
 effect to the said Convention;
BE   it  enacted  by Parliament  in the  Fifty-first Year of  the  Republic of India as follows:
CHAPTER I
PRELIMINARY
1. (1) This Act may be called the Biological Diversity Act, 2000.
(2) It extends to the whole of India.
(3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification
 in the Official Gazette, appoint:
Provided that different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Act and any
 reference in any such provision to the commencement of this Act shall be construed as a
 reference to the coming into force of that provision.
2. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires -
(a)
    "benefit claimers" means the conservers of biological resources their by-products,
 creators and holders of knowledge and information relating to the use of such biological
 resources, innovations and practices associated with such use and application;
 (b) "biological diversity" means the variability among living organisms from all sources and
 the ecological complexes of which they are part and includes diversity within species or between
 species and of eco-systems;

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
Biodiversity encompasses the variety of all life on earth. India is one of the 12 mega
 biodiversity countries of the world. With only 2.5% of the land area, India already accounts for
 7.8% of the recorded species of the world. India is equally rich in traditional and indigenous
 knowledge, both coded and informal.
2. India is a Party of the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992). The main objectives of the
 Convention are:
(i) Conservation of biological diversity;
(ii) Sustainable use of its components;
(iii) Fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of utilisation of genetic resources.
 
3. Recognizing the sovereign rights of States to use their own biological resources, the
 Convention expects the Parties to facilitate access to genetic resources by other Parties for
 environmentally sound purposes subject to national legislation and on mutually agreed upon
 terms (Articles 3 and 15). Article 8(j) of the Convention recognizes contributions of local and
 indigenous communities to the conservation and sustainable utilisation of biological diversity

4. Biodiversity is a multi-disciplinary subject involving diverse sectoral activities and actions. The
 stakeholders in biological diversity include the Central Government, State Government,
 institutions of local self-government, scientific and technical institutions, experts, non-
governmental organizations, industry, etc. One of the major challenges before India lies in
 adopting an instrument which helps realise the objectives of equitable sharing of benefits
 enshrined in the Convention on Biological Diversity.
 
5. After an extensive and intensive consultation process involving the stakeholders, the Central
 Government has decided to bring a legislation with the following salient features: -
 
(i) to regulate access to biological resources of the country with the purpose of
 securing equitable share in benefits arising out of the use of biological resources;
 and associated knowledge relating to biological resources;
(ii) to conserve and sustainably use biological diversity;
(iii) to respect and protect knowledge of local communities related to biodiversity;
(iv) to secure sharing of benefits with local people as conservers of biological
 resources and holders of knowledge and information relating to the use of
 biological resources;
(v) conservation and development of areas important from the standpoint of
 biological diversity by declaring them as biological diversity heritage sites;
(vi) protection and rehabilitation of threatened species;
(vii) involvement of institutions of self-government in the broad scheme of the
 implementation of the Act through constitution of committees.
6. The proposed legislation primarily addresses the issue concerning access to genetic resources
 and associated knowledge by foreign individuals, institutions or companies, and equitable sharing
 of benefits arising out of the use of these resources and knowledge to the country and the people.
 In order to safeguard the interests of the local people, vaid and hakims and to allow research by
 Indian citizens within the country, the following exceptions are proposed: -
(i) Free access to biological resources for use within India for any purpose other
 than commercial use for Indian people.
(ii) Use of biological resources by vaids and hakims.
(iii) Free access to the Indian citizens to use biological resources within the country
 for research purposes.
(iv) Collaborative research through government sponsored or government approved
 institutions subject to overall policy guidelines and approval of the Central
 Government
.
 7. It is proposed to have National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and
 Biodiversity Management Committees.
(a) The National Biodiversity Authority will deal with matters relating to requests
 for access by foreign individuals, institutions or companies, and all matters relating
 to transfer of results of research to any foreigner; imposition of terms and
 conditions to secure equitable sharing of benefits and approval for seeking any form
 of Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) in or outside India for an invention based on
 research or information pertaining to a biological resource obtained from India.
(b) State Biodiversity Boards will deal with matters relating to access by Indians for
 commercial purposes and restrict any activity which violates the objectives of
 conservation, sustainable use and equitable sharing of benefits.
(c) Biodiversity Management Committees will be set up by institutions of self-
government in their respective areas for conservation, sustainable use,
 documentation of biodiversity and chronicling of knowledge relating to
 biodiversity. Biodiversity Management Committees shall be consulted by the
 National Biodiversity Authority and State Biodiversity Boards on matters related to
 use of biological resources and associated knowledge within their jurisdiction

 Biodiversity Fund will be laid before the State Legislature.
Clause 48- This clause stipulates that the National Biodiversity Authority in discharge of its
 functions and duties shall be bound by the directions of the Central Government.
Clause 49- This clause stipulates that the State Biodiversity Board in discharge of its functions
 and duties shall be bound by the directions of the State Government.
Clause 50 - This clause sets out the detailed procedure for settlement of disputes between State
 Biodiversity Boards; proceedings before the National Authority shall be deemed to be a judicial
 proceeding for the purpose of section 196 of the Indian Penal Code and the National Authority
 shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for the purposes of section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the
 Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Clause 51- This clause states that the members, officers and other employees of the National
 Authority or State Biodiversity Boards shall be deemed to be public servants.
Clause 52- This clause provides for protection of action taken in good faith by the Central
 Government or the State Government officers and employees of the said governments, members,
 officers or employees of the National Biodiversity Authority or the State Biodiversity Board,
 from any suit, prosecution or other legal proceedings.
Clause 53 – This clause provides for penalties for contravening clauses 3, 4 and 6. The penalty
 will be imprisonment for a term which may extend to 5 years or fine which may extend to Rs. 10
 lakhs or both; and that penalty for contravention of the provisions of clause (7) and sub-clause (1)
 of clause 24 shall be imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or fine which may
 extend to Rs. 5 lakhs or both.
Clause 54 - This clause provides for penalty for contravention of directions or orders of the
 Central Government, the State Government, the National Biodiversity Authority and the State
 Biodiversity Boards.
Clause 55 – This clause contains provisions for offences by companies. This clause seeks to
 provide that where a person committing offence is a company, every person responsible in the
 company for the conduct of its business will be liable; where a person accused proves that the
 offence was committed without his knowledge he will not be liable. However, where it is proved
 that an offence has been committed with the consent or connivance or is attributable to the
 neglect of any director, manager, secretary or any other officer of the company, he shall be
 deemed to be guilty of the offence.
Clause 56- This clause provides that the offences under this Act shall be recognizable and non-
bail able.
Clause 57- This clause states that the provisions of the proposed legislation shall have overriding
 effect on all other laws for the time being in force or anything inconsistent with the proposed
 legislation contained in any instrument.
Clause 58- This clause stipulates that the Central Government may give directions to the State
 Governments for execution any of the provisions of this Act.
Clause 59- This clause provides that no court shall take cognizance of any offence under this Act
 or rules/ regulations made thereunder except for complaints made by National Biodiversity
 Authority or State Biodiversity Boards.
Clause 60 – This clause empowers the Central Government to make rules to carry out the

Clause 61- This clause empowers the State Government to make rules to carry out the provisions
 of the proposed legislation, enumerates the various matters in respect of which such rules may be

Clause 62- This clause empowers the National Biodiversity Authority to make regulations
 consistent with the provisions of the proposed legislation and the rules made thereunder. Such
 regulations are required to be made with the previous approval of the Central Government and by

Clause 63-This clause empowers the Central Government to remove difficulties which may arise
 in giving effect to the provisions of the proposed legislation by order published in the Official

 power can be exercised only within two years from the commencement of the proposed
 legislation. Every such order shall be required to be laid before Parliament.
 
FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
Clause 8 provides for setting up of a Statutory Authority to be known as the National
 Biodiversity Authority at Chennai. The Authority may decide in the future to establish offices in
 other places in India as envisaged under clause 8(3) of the Bill. The recurring expenditure
 towards salary, allowances and other expenditure relating to Chairperson, members and other
 officers and employees of the Authority appointed under Clause 14 will be of the order of Rs. 10
 lakhs per annum. The other recurring expenditure by way of rent, maintenance, meetings, office
 expenses and contingency etc, will be of the order of Rs. 80 lakhs per annum. Non-recurring
 expenditure on establishment, office equipment, vehicles, etc. will be approximately of the order
 of Rs. 50 lakhs.
MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Clause 60 of the Bill empowers the Central Government to make rules by notification in the
 official Gazette for carrying out the purposes of the proposed legislation. Sub-clause (2) of that
 clause enumerates the matters with respect to which rules may be made under the proposed
 legislation. These matters inter-alia relate to the terms of office; the salary and allowances and
 conditions of the Chairperson and members of the National Biodiversity Authority; powers and
 duties of Chairperson, transaction of business of the National Biodiversity Authority, form of
 application and payment of fees for undertaking certain activities; the procedure for adjudication,
 etc.
2. Clause 61 of the Bill empowers the State Governments to make rules by notification in the
 official Gazette for carrying out purposes of this proposed legislation. Sub-clause (2) of that
 clause enumerates the various matters with respect to which rules may be made under this
 legislation. These matters inter alia relate to the form in which the prior intimation shall be given;
 rules for the management and conservation of heritage sites; management of the Local
 Biodiversity Fund, etc.
3. Clause 62 of the Bill empowers the National Biodiversity Authority to make regulations with
 the previous approval of the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette.
4. The rules and regulations made under the proposed legislation shall be required to be laid
 before Parliament.
5. The aforesaid matters in respect of which rules, regulations may be made or framed relate to
 matters of procedure or administrative detail and it is not practicable to provide for them in the
 Bill itself. The delegation of legislative power is, therefore of a normal character.

(Para 35)
Action Taken by the Department
Necessity for the Programme:
The necessity for undertaking the Himalayan Glaciology Programme has been felt by DST because the study of Himalayan
 Glaciers is important and significant due to the following factors:
(a)  Glaciers & snow fields are an important source of fresh water and their melt water support the flow of Indus, Ganga and
 Brahmaputra rivers and their tributaries. It is important to know the behaviour of glaciers for planning hydroelectric
 power projects, roads, and other utility services of national importance such as floods/avalanche monitoring and
 management. Glacier studies are being carried out all over the world for similar purposes.
(b) The climate and weather pattern of India is greatly influenced by Himalaya and Himalayan glaciers and snow fields.
 Glacier fluctuation has been identified as one of the Geo-indicators useful to assess the geological aspect of global
 climate change.  It was identified in Agenda 21 of the 1992 United Nations Rio Conference on the Environment.    
 Therefore, no country in the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river basins can afford to ignore the glaciers.
(c)  Glacier advance or recession is an important environmental parameter. Glaciers are sensitive barometers of climate
 change, growing and dwarfing in response to the changes in temperature and snowfall. So, the glacier fluctuations of
 past and present  serve as valuable source of  information for regional and global climate, melt water flow,
 environmental change in mountain region and their adjoining   plains. Being intimately connected with various
 geological processes, glaciers provide insight into the geology of Himalayas.
(d)  The valley glaciers and other related formations are part of the geomorphic pattern of the Himalaya.
DST’s Enthusiasm and Zeal for the Programme:
DST is coordinating/promoting studies on Himalayan Glaciers as also providing financial assistance for research and
 development activities so as to generate a strong R&D database for future studies  on the  subject.  DST has been  playing a
 pivotal  role to  provide a platform for  its
 sister organizations and academic/research institutions for pursuing research in
 identified priority areas and undertaking coordinated multi- institutional and multi-disciplinary research activities in selected
 major glaciers of national importance.  DST is very much keen to make all out effort to chalk out strategies so as to
 stimulate/encourage scientists and creating scientific temper which in turn may strengthen the Himalayan Glaciology
 programme.
Some of the important activities to be implemented by DST in the near future are as follows:-
In addition to on-going activities, DST has proposed a multidisciplinary and multi-institutional coordinated project to study
 the Dokriani Bamak Glacier. The project is now under consideration of DST funding. There are 8 research institutions involved
 in this project to study various aspects of the Dokriani Bamak Glacier.
DST has also proposed collaboration at international level to take joint studies and training of manpower. The proposal is
 being taken up by the International Division of DST with other Central Asian Region countries. ,
A project on "National Snow Science Workshop" to be organized by SASE, Chandigarh, is also under consideration of DST
 funding. The workshop will provide an opportunity to the scientists of the country to express their views and come out with
 future strategies in the field of glaciology.
As in the past, the emphasis will be laid on manpower development. Geological Survey of India (GSI) has trained a number
 of scientists in last five years involving DST support. Efforts will be made to organize field-oriented training programme for the
 promising young scientists who then could take up research activities.
Glaciological research has been pursued for long in the country with different levels of success. These studies were more or
 less carried out with limited objectives. Now, it has become very clear that the science of glaciology should be pursued in the
 country by a totally dedicated Centre. With this aim, a proposal to set up a National Centre for Field Operations and Research
 on Himalayan Glaciology (NCFOR-HG) has been prepared. The National Centre would strive to generate a strong in-house
 research base as well as a network of state-of-the-art laboratories mid field operation facilities which will also be available to
 researchers from other centers and Universities across the country for their investigations. The National Centre will bring
 holistic approach to the Himalayan glaciological research in the country and provide much needed data base for formulation of
 national policies on natural resource management in glacier regions of the country.
Efforts are on to disseminate information and to popularize the programme widely among scientists of the country. To
 achieve this target, a Brochure on Himalayan Glaciology is likely to come out shortly. A website on the programme is also
 being -planned to be accessed through INTERNET. Similarly, periodical publication of a News Letter on Himalayan
 Glaciology is under consideration.

Recommendation
 While the Committee appreciates that Department of Science and Technology is choosing herbs for development of
 drugs with a view to find a cure for many diseases affecting the society, the Committee is constrained to observe that not
 much is being done in the field of traditional systems of medicines in the country whereas some of the other countries

Another point which the Committee would like the  DST to bear in mind that the chances of bringing the private
 sector or, for that matter the industry on a common platform for research on any other form of collaboration, are
 indeed remote because the industry does not work from a welfare point of view. Rather profit is its motive. In fact the
 Committee is constrained to observe that the commercialization of human suffering diseases appears to be becoming the
 order of the day in private hospitals/clinics etc. This trends needs to be discouraged.
The Committee would like to reiterate that it would be indeed futile to merely add drugs to the ones already existing
 in the country. Efforts should always be aimed to develop drugs that tend to wipe out the diseases and not merely cure

 be carried out in more & more Indian languages. Besides, in view of the role played by HAM radio during the recent
 Gujarat earthquake as well as Orissa cyclone, it should be popularized among people so that they are encouraged to
 develop and use it as hobby. Besides, equipment for HAM radio be made available at cheaper prices.
(Para 48)
Action Taken by the Department
 (a) Vigyan Prasar has already initiated efforts towards strengthening of the publication activities in various vernacular
 languages on relevant S&T topics and issues.
 
(b)  Vigyan Prasar has initiated efforts for popularization of HAM radio. In particulars, the activity will be initiated in States
 which are particularly prone to natural disasters, say Uttranchal, Orissa, Himachal Pradesh, U.P. and Gujarat. Vigyan
 Prasar intends to establish HAM radio club stations and run training programmes to help prospective hams to clear the
 Amateur station operator's certificate examination conducted by the Ministry of Communication. Passing this
 examination is a pre- requisite for obtaining a license for setting up a HAM radio Station. Efforts are also on to make
 HAM radio equipments available at affordable prices.
(c)  Vigyan Prasar Network (VIPNET) Science Clubs activity is expected to grow significantly into a movement for
 popularization of S&T especially in rural areas in the days to come.
Comments

 augmented as per the recommendation of the Committee. In the absence of the contrary, the Committee presumes that the
 allocation has been made as recommended by the Committee.

In recommending the enhanced budgetary allocation for Vigyan Prasar the Committee has been guided by the
 imperative need to spread and inculcate scientific temper. The programme should be suitably modified on the basis of
 experience gained and the feedback received from the participants and others. Shortage of funds should not be allowed
 to stand in the way of such programmes.
(Para 49)

The programmes of Vigyan Prasar are aimed at spreading and inculcating scientific temper alongwith dissemination of
 scientific information/software. Vigyan Prasar continues to put in efforts to modify and improve its programmes based on the
 experience and feed-back received from the participants to inculcate scientific temper among them. In training programmes,
 efforts are made to follow the discovery approach enabling the participants to arrive at a conclusion through his/her own efforts
 with resource persons playing only a catalytic role. Several publications and learning/teaching modules/kits also reflect the
 same guiding principle. This is and would be a continuing process.
Comments
The Committee commends the efforts being made by the Department in the popularization of S&T related activities.

Recommendation
      The Committee notes the work being done by the S&T wings in Indian missions abroad. The Committee would have
 appreciated some more details about the complement of staff, budgetary support provided to these S&T wings. Likewise
 whether there are any plans to open more of such wings in the Missions located in some other countries. The Committee
 will consider their functioning in greater  details at a later stage.  The Committee have been
 receiving journal on S&T in
 Germany, published monthly from S&T wing in Berlin. The Committee expects that such journals brought out by other
 missions be made available to it.
(Para 51)

Currently there are only four science wings abroad i.e, Germany, Japan, Russia & USA. Each Science Wing is headed by a
 Scientific Attaché with Personal Assistant and Junior Scientific Assistant as a supporting staff. So far, total budgetary support
 of about Rs.4 crores each year is being provided to these science wings abroad. There is an emergent need to create scientific
 attaché positions in other appropriate countries, like China, UK, Latin Americas and Central Asian region for intensifying the
 collaborative efforts. A number of countries are coming forward for collaboration in S&T with India for a variety of reasons.
 Better counseling from our own persons in the country of reference would highly facilitate quick utilization of opportunities
 and chalking out of effective and realistic programmes. This has been reflected in the report of the Working Group on
 International Cooperation in Science & Technology for the Formulation of the Tenth Five Year Plan.
Comments
While the Committee has started receiving Journals/Reports etc. on S&T from our Embassies located at Germany,
 Japan & Russia, it is yet to receive such publications from our Embassy in United States of America.
Recommendation
While considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science & Technology and assessing the progress of
 various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee found the discrepancy in the total
 amount of the Demands for Grants for Department of Science & Technology. The Expenditure Budget 2001-02 (vol.2)
 shows that the total Demand for Grants as sought by DST is Rs.823.97 crores whereas the document containing detailed

 Department clarified that this is due to receipts from various resources.
The Committee therefore recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs.829.62 crores, as sought by the
 Department of Science & Technology for the year 2001-2002 under demand No.68 nay be approved.
(Para 52)
Action Taken by the Department
The Demands for Grants (Demand No. 68) for Rs.829.62 crores in respect of Department of Science & Technology for the
 financial year 2001-2002 have since been voted by the Parliament.

R E P O R T
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development on the
 recommendations contained in the Eighty-eight Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Ocean
 Development which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 20th April, 2001 and laid on the table of Lok Sabha on the 20 th
 April, 2001.  There are eighteen recommendations contained in the eighty-eight Report of the Committee. Action Taken
 notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 23rd October, 2001.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the
 Department of Ocean Development are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2001-02
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that in view of considerable reduction in the Budgetary support at RE level last year, it
 should be possible for the Department to manage with the reduced budgetary support this year.  To that end the
 Committee brings on record the assurance given by the Department in reply to Question 1 of the Questionnaire (See
 Appendix) that the present outlay will not hold up the execution of any programme.
                                                                                                                                  (Para 14)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department is grateful for the concern shown by the Committee with regard to the reduction in the budgetary
 support for the current year.  The Department would like to re-assure the Committee that the present outlay will not hold up
 the execution of any programme.
Comments:
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
In the context of delay in the Commissioning the Technology Demonstration Pilot Plant for extraction of metals
 from Poly Metallic Nodules at Hindustan Zinc Ltd., at Udaipur, HZL (U), which  was to be commissioned in
 October, 2000 and the Pilot Plant which was expected to be commissioned off Tuticorin coast in September-October,
 2000, the Committee observes that such delays result in cost escalations.  Besides, they reflect on the Departments’
 efficiency to plan things meticulously.  Such delays need to be avoided.
                                                                                                            (Para 15)
Action Taken by the Department
It is submitted that the initiation of the project was delayed for few months due to delay in the finalization of the contract
 for the erection & commissioning of the plant by HZL (U). The plant is now scheduled for commissioning in October, 2001
 without any cost escalation.
As regards the commissioning of the floating OTEC Plant off Tuticorin, there were delays in completing the two main
 components viz., the plant barge and the sea water system. These delays were due to delayed supply by vendors and some
 teething problem during fabrication.  Finally, however, when the sea water systems were being deployed there was a mishap
 resulting in loss of the pipelines. This has caused a set back to the project which is now expected to be commissioned only
 by mid 2002.  The Committee’s directions have been noted and every effort would be made to ensure completion of projects
 as per schedule.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that steps would be taken to ensure such delays do not reoccur and

 timely completion of projects is carried out.  The Committee would also like to know whether cost escalation would
 take place in commissioning of the floating OTEC Plant off Tuticorin if commissioned by mid of 2002 and how it will
 be met out. 
MAJOR DISPROPORTIONATE VARIATIONS AND REASONS
Recommendation
As regards the reasons advanced for non-utilisation of the budgetary support in respect of continental shelf and
 Poly Metallic Nodules programme, the Committee is concernd with the delays in finalizing the contracts and
 observes such delays could have been avoided.
(Para 17)
Action Taken by the Department
In relation to continental shelf programme the delay in finalizing the contract was on account of
(i)
                  new understanding about the geology of Laxmi Basin in Arabian Sea and thereby changing the technical
 parameters of the tender as per the provisions of Scientific and Technical Guidelines of the Commission and
(ii)                delay in initiating the discussion with Sri Lanka which are crucial in implementing the provisions of Law of
 the Sea.
While the technical parameters for the tender are under the final stages of confirmation, Ministry of External Affairs is
 taking up the matter with Sri Lanka, which is critical for undertaking survey.
Comments
The Committee feels that the Department should pursue with Ministry of External affairs for taking up the
 matter with the Sri Lankan government to reach an agreement so that any delay on this account is minimized.
NON-PLAN PROGRAMMES
Recommendation
As regards the difficulties being faced by the Department on the non-plan side with regard to the payments to the
 Shipping Corporation of India for the operation of the Research Vessels “Sagar Kanya” and Sagar Sampada”, while the
 committee is all out for reduction of non-plan expenditure, but in view of the seriousness of the expenditure for Research
 Vessels, the Committee feels that it is a kind of committed expenditure and the Department should not be compelled to
 dither on its commitments, the Committee recommends that the budgetary support on this count be suitably augmented now
 or at least at RE stage or else the research vessels may remain idle and consequently the research effort may suffer which
 would not be healthy development.                                                                                                                            (Para 19)
Action Taken by the Department
The non-plan BE 2001-02 for FORV Sagar Sampada is Rs. 10.31 crore.  Taking into consideration the mandatory need
 for dry dock repairs of the vessel during 2001-02 and the critical need to upgrade the scientific facilities on board, the BE
 under FORV non-plan head 2001-02 need to be enhanced by at least Rs. 1 crore at the RE stage.  The non-plan BE 2001-02
 for ORV Sagar Kanya is Rs. 13.12 crore.   
Comments
The Committee observes that the Department should have indicated the action taken for augmenting the budgetary
 requirements.  The Department should now take up the matter with the Ministries/Departments concerned for suitably
 augmenting the budgetary support.
POLAR SCIENCES
Antarctic Expedition
Recommendation
The Committee feels that the baseline data collected by National Hydrographic Office (NHO) should be analysed in
 consultation with National Institutions like Geological Survey of India, National Institute of Oceanography, National
 Geophysical Research Institute etc., for estimating the foot of the slope and 2500 m isobath in accordance with the format
 specified in the guidelines of the Commission.
                                                                                                                              (Para 28)
Action Taken by the Department

 Hydrographic Office, National Geophysical Research Institute, Geological Survey of India, National Institute of
 Oceanography and National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research were also present.  NHO indicated that the
 bathymetric data gathered by them and the Geological Survey of India have already been compiled, reconciled and
